title: Project overview
text: CI npm License: MIT Node 22+ A zero-dependency UI library with server rendering, built for agents to write, check and maintain. Modern UI frameworks optimize for human ergonomics: implicit conventions, flexible APIs, and multiple ways to express the same component. For an LLM coding agent forty turns into a session, that flexibility is a trap. As context decays, agents hallucinate non-existent props, mix framework idioms, and introduce subtle state bugs that require a real browser to catch. agent-ui inverts this design. It gives agents a closed, declarative JSON grammar authored through typed JavaScript builders, paired with strict, transactional state namespaces. There is exactly one valid shape for every construct. If an agent makes a mistake, the runtime rejects it immediately with an error message that gives the exact syntax fix. And because the entire UI, state tree, and interactive surface are plain data, an agent can render, inspect, and test every page headlessly in Node in milliseconds. Strictness for the machine does not compromise the output for humans. Pages map to real URLs, render on the server, and mount in the browser with a 13 KB gzipped runtime, zero virtual DOM o

title: Why This Exists
parts: An LLM agent is fast and tireless, but its context decays: it produces confident near-misses—React conventions in a non-React codebase, hallucinated options, or subtle state mutations—and it cannot see the browser unless you wire up heavy headless tooling.
agent-ui keeps what a UI framework must do—keeping the DOM in sync with state quickly and predictably—and wraps it in a closed grammar that a machine can verify without a browser.

title: Core Guarantees
parts: Closed Grammar & Builder Syntax: The UI is a pure JSON specification. You author it using thin builders (div(...), button(...), state(...)) that look like standard markup functions and return plain JSON. Because the UI is data, it can be validated, diffed, patched and generated.

One Valid Form for Everything: A page, an endpoint, and a build option each have one fixed shape. There is no shorthand or overloading. Unknown keys are rejected immediately, and typos return actionable "Did you mean?" suggestions.

Errors the agent can fix on the next turn: Every validation error names the exact path, the violation, and the valid fix. When an agent makes a mistake, the error message in its terminal gives it the exact syntax needed to self-correct on the next turn.

Isolated, Transactional State: State lives in flat, JSON-serializable namespaces and is mutated only by named, typed actions. Cross-namespace updates go through declared calls. If any part of an action chain throws, the entire transaction rolls back. Every action is logged for deterministic replay.

Headless verification & cost budgets: State, derived values, the interactive surface, and the rendered DOM tree are inspectable as JSON in Node. measureAction and assertCost count exact DOM writes, effect runs, and state changes. Build budgets turn pages that exceed size or node limits into hard CI errors.
Zero Dependencies: The runtime, compiler, dev server, SSR engine, and test runner use only Node's standard library and native browser APIs. package.json has zero dependencies or devDependencies.

title: Performance & Footprint
parts: Design priorities, in strict order: performance, accuracy, size.

No Virtual DOM: One state binding compiles to one effect that writes to one DOM property. There is no VDOM diffing overhead. Toggling a row in a list costs exactly three DOM mutations at any list size.

13 KB gzipped: The production runtime is about 47 KB, 13 KB gzipped, with readable symbols—only comments and whitespace are stripped. A real minifier plugs into transform, and source maps (sourceMaps) work with or without it: the minifier's map is followed back to your files. Framework code, each npm package and your app's code are separate chunks, so a deploy of your app leaves the rest cached. See docs/BUILD.md.

Declared List Shapes: Lists declare their item schema up front. Typos in {item} bindings fail at mount, malformed writes fail in development, and a validate hook lets external validators like Zod verify items at runtime.

title: Two Ways to Adopt
parts: You can drop agent-ui into an existing backend as isolated islands, or let it manage page routing and SSR.

As a Library (Islands): Keep your existing server, router, and build pipeline. renderPage() renders a spec on the server, stateScriptHtml() serializes the state, and readServerState() + app() mount it in the browser. See examples/islands for a plain node:http server running two interactive islands with no build step.

With the Page Model: A folder under pages/ maps 1:1 to a URL (pages/event/[id]/page.js serves /event/:id). agent-ui build bundles each page as an independent entry point so clients only download what that route imports. createSsrHandler renders pages per request inside your host server.
What it is not: A web server or a monolithic application framework. Sessions, authentication, file uploads, WebSockets, compression, and caching belong to your host server (SECURITY.md).

title: Architecture: The Six Building Blocks
parts: Everything an application does fits into six primitives:
You Need                                          Primitive                   What It Gives You
State and behavior for a UI domain                Namespace (inside an App)   Owns plain JSON state, pure derive functions and synchronous actions.

Network IO, timers, DOM events, 3rd-party libs    Plugin                      (api) => void run once after mount. Reads via api.watch, writes via api.dispatch so all side effects become logged actions.
A routable URL                                    Page                        A folder under pages/ containing page.js (behavior, plugins, status, head) and view.js (the spec).

Persistent layout across page navigations         Shell                       A second app (defineShell) wrapping a page (e.g. header with cart badge, audio player). Reads page state one-way via reads.
An interactive widget in a server-rendered page   Island                      A standalone app() mounted into a host DOM element without the pages/ router.

Cross-app communication                           syncApps                    Watches keys in one app and dispatches an action in another. Unidirectional, validated at setup and logged on the receiver.

Plugin           Import                         Use It When
withResources    @ehtb/agent-ui/resources       A namespace fetches async data (resources)

title: State Management & Data Flow
parts: State flows strictly one way. The UI cannot mutate state directly, and state only reaches the DOM through explicit bindings.

Strict Encapsulation: Inside a namespace, actions read their own keys directly (store.get('draft')) and read other namespaces via qualified names (get('search.query')). Under the hood, each qualified key is a signal. State is immutable; development builds Object.freeze state trees so accidental in-place mutations throw immediately.
Memoized Derivations: derive holds pure functions of state. Results that are structurally equal to their previous evaluation preserve object references, preventing downstream re-renders.

Atomic Cross-Namespace Calls: When an action needs to update another namespace, it declares the target in calls and invokes call('search.clear', {}). If any step throws, all state changes across all namespaces in that dispatch are rolled back.

Deterministic Replay & Batched Timing: Every completed outer action is recorded in the action log, enabling ui.replay(log) for session reproduction, headless regression tests, and state preservation across hot reloads. State updates are synchronous after dispatch; derived(), outline(), and DOM mutations batch into a single microtask resolved via await ui.settle().

title: Known Architectural Constraints
parts: To keep the mental model small for agents and the runtime fast, several boundaries are enforced by design:

Flat Namespaces: Namespaces are one level deep (namespace.key), and calls only go one level deep (a called action cannot call another namespace). Heavy cross-calling is a signal to restructure your state or use derive.

No Hidden Component State: Ephemeral UI state (like an edit-mode toggle or input draft) lives in the store. Per-row UI state (open, selected) is declared once on the namespace via rowState and read via rowState('namespace.field').

Full List Derivation (No Virtualization): Derived lists recompute in full when inputs change, and {item} bindings read the innermost loop (outer loops are aliased with as and read via row('name.field')). This performs well up to thousands of rows, but will bottleneck at tens of thousands.
No Template Formatting Syntax: Numbers, dates, and currencies are formatted in derive using standard Intl APIs and memoizeItem, keeping the view grammar closed.
Synchronous, Serializable State: State must be pure JSON (no Date, Map, or class instances). Actions are strictly synchronous; all async work happens in plugins.

Destructive Hydration: On mount, the client replaces the server-rendered DOM tree rather than adopting nodes. Pre-mount user input and focus state are preserved via data-id, but scroll offsets inside nested containers and running CSS animations reset on mount.

Strict Bundler Dialect: To keep the built-in bundler zero-dependency and fast, source files must use relative imports with file extensions, named exports only, no circular dependencies, and no export *. Third-party packages that violate this (e.g., zod, Tiptap) are imported via a pre-bundled vendor file (docs/BUILD.md).

title: Setting Up Your Coding Agent
parts: When using Claude Code, Cursor, OpenCode, or another coding agent in a project with agent-ui:

Run npx agent-ui init once. This injects the core syntax rules directly into your repository's root AGENTS.md so the agent loads them automatically (since agents rarely crawl node_modules unprompted).
Point the agent to node_modules/@ehtb/agent-ui/docs/AGENT-RULES.md and GUIDE.md.

Let the agent use npx agent-ui explain [topic] and npx agent-ui check in its tool loop. Every recipe in cookbook/ (dialogs, comboboxes, drag-reorder lists, async resources, SVG icons) is executable and printable directly in the terminal via agent-ui explain.

title: CLI Reference
parts: Command                   Description
agent-ui build            Builds production assets to dist/ (hashed filenames, comments stripped, validator omitted). Pass --dev to retain the validator, or --static to pre-render static HTML files.
agent-ui dev              Starts the dev server with hot-reload (swaps edited pages in place while replaying action logs to preserve state).
agent-ui serve            Starts a local test server (http://localhost:8080) for SSR pages, JSON APIs, and form posts. Not intended for production exposure—deploy behind your host server or CDN.
agent-ui check            Renders every page in development mode headlessly, verifying all specs, links, data shapes, and size budgets at once.
agent-ui explain [name]   Prints the canonical implementation for a cookbook recipe or grammar rule directly to stdout. Lists all available topics if called without arguments.
agent-ui schema           Emits the complete JSON Schema for the UI spec grammar.
agent-ui init             Writes the condensed agent instructions into the host project's AGENTS.md.
agent-ui --help prints the command list; agent-ui --version prints the package version.

title: Type Safety Without a Build Step
parts: The framework's source code in src/ is plain, untranspiled JavaScript so that when an agent inspects node_modules/@ehtb/agent-ui/src, what it reads is 1:1 with what runs.
Alongside every JavaScript module, the package ships hand-written .d.ts and .d.mts declarations (ui.d.ts, pages.d.ts, build/config.d.mts).

Zero-Config Editor Support: Plain JS projects get full autocomplete and type checking simply by adding // @ts-check. TypeScript projects get full type resolution without needing a framework compile step.
Readable Contracts: pages.d.ts fits on a single screen and states the exact shape a caller may pass, free of internal implementation noise.

Docs tested against the code: Type definitions are tested via test/types/check.js, and documentation comments are tested against the codebase—every file path, CLI flag, and import name mentioned in the docs is asserted by the test suite.

title: Browser Support, Stability & Maturity
parts: Runtime Targets: Requires Node 22+ on the server and modern evergreen browsers (Chrome/Edge 93+, Firefox 92+, Safari 15.4+ — any environment supporting Object.hasOwn). Code is shipped as modern ES modules without transpilation bloat.

Versioning: Currently 0.x. Minor releases may adjust the grammar or APIs, with migration paths documented in CHANGELOG.md. Starting at 1.0.0, the spec grammar, exported APIs, CLI flags, build config keys, and error codes (AUI + 4 digits) will follow strict Semantic Versioning.

Maturity: This is young software. The architectural thesis—that a closed, self-explaining grammar measurably reduces agent error rates over long sessions—is a hypothesis documented in docs/DESIGN.md. Because LLMs have not seen agent-ui in pre-training, the design compensates with a minimal surface area, agent-ui init, and runtime error messages that teach the syntax on the fly.

title: Agent rules
text: This is the short operating manual for an agent that writes an app with agent-ui. Read it before you write a page. Then read GUIDE.md (how pages, URLs, APIs and forms fit together) and use API.md as the reference. agent-ui explain prints a recipe from cookbook/ or the one valid form of a part of the grammar. The AGENTS.md at the root of the framework repository is for work on the framework itself, not for building an app; it is not published.

title: 1. Start here
parts: Run agent-ui explain and copy the recipe closest to the task. A recipe is a page that agent-ui check renders and the tests drive; start from it instead of from memory of another framework. agent-ui explain <name> prints the files.

A page is a URL and two files: pages/<url>/page.js (behavior) and pages/<url>/view.js (content). / is pages/page.js; /event/:id is pages/event/[id]/page.js; /docs/*path is pages/docs/[...path]/page.js.
Change state through named, typed actions only. The spec holds no logic.
Run agent-ui check before you finish: it renders every page whose URL has no parameters, validates every finished spec, and reports spec, link and data problems together. Fix every line it prints.
Test with the agent API: dispatch actions, await ui.settle(), assert ui.state(), ui.derived(), ui.outline() and ui.tree(), and call assertNoErrors(ui).
Every validator message has the place, the problem and the fix, and an unknown key gets a "Did you mean" suggestion. Fix the spec at the path it names; do not suppress the check.

title: 2. The model
parts: The UI is a JSON spec, written with the builders of @ehtb/agent-ui/spec. The builders return the JSON the runtime, the server and the tests see.
State is plain JSON in namespaces. Every state key, derived value and action belongs to one namespace (todos.draft, todos.add). Replace values, never mutate them.
Only actions write state, and an action writes only its own namespace. Cross-namespace changes go through declared calls.
Everything external is a plugin: network, timers, window events, an editor. Plugins talk to the app only through api.watch and api.dispatch, so every state change is a logged action.
Every list has a stable, unique key. A duplicate drops the later item; agent-ui check and the mount check report it.
The flow is one way: state, then derive, then spec bindings, then one DOM property. Events go back only as [actionName, args] handlers.

Cross-namespace changes go through declared calls. Everything external is a plugin: network, timers, window events, an editor. Plugins talk to the app only through api.watch and api.dispatch, so every state change is a logged action. Every list has a stable, unique key. A duplicate drops the later item; agent-ui check and the mount check report it. The flow is one way: state, then derive, then spec bindings, then one DOM property. Events go back only as [actionName, args] handlers.

title: 3. A page
parts: page.js is behavior only:

view.js exports view (required) and optionally layout, pending and the content of the shell. In a production build, only the server and the build import view.js: the browser gets the finished spec as data, so it never downloads the builders. A development build imports view.js in the browser too, so the spec is rebuilt from source.

Styles: pages/<url>/page.css is that page's CSS; pages/style.css is every page's CSS. Both may start with @import "./file.css"; for CSS shared with a few pages; the build links a file imported by a subset of pages only to those pages (BUILD.md, "CSS imports"). Never import CSS from page.js, view.js or a component: those run in Node.
Keep window and fetch injectable where you write a helper, so tests run headless.

Server state, headers and a session. A page renders from its own state. The render server (createSsrHandler) reads the request once and gives it to api.handle, api.handleForm, initialStateFor, stateForBrowser, transformResponse and fetchFunction(url, init, request); initialStateFor(request) returns public state the page starts from, stateForBrowser(state, request) chooses what the document's state script carries (a key only the server reads is left out), and transformResponse(request, { status, headers, body }) returns { headers?, body? } to add response headers or rewrite the body (for example a CSP nonce). The framework has no session store, login flow, authorization or CSP policy: keep a session token in an HttpOnly cookie set by the API or a form, put only public data in initialStateFor, and check the cookie or CSRF token in the handler that changes state. A page cannot set response headers; API and form outcomes and transformResponse can set a cookie. The host sends vary: cookie or cache-control: private from transformResponse for a page whose state depends on the visitor; no-cache alone does not separate visitors in a shared cache. See GUIDE.md, "A session, a CSP and response headers".

title: 4. State and actions
parts: Names are identifiers: letters and digits, starting with a lowercase letter, no dots or dashes.
Argument types are 'string', 'number', 'boolean', 'json'; pass exactly the declared arguments in a handler.
derive functions are pure and synchronous. Own keys are plain (get('items')); another namespace is read qualified (get('search.query')), never written.

To change another namespace, list its action in calls and run call('search.clear', {}). The owner does the writing, one level only, and the whole thing is one log entry that is undone if any part throws.
Keep state JSON-serializable: strings, numbers, booleans, null, arrays, plain objects. No functions, Date, Map, Set or class instances.
No Date.now() or Math.random() in an action: replay must be deterministic. Counters and ids live in state.

A row's own state (open, selected, a draft) is rowState in the namespace, written with store.setRow(id, { open: true }) and read with rowState('todos.open'). Call clearRow from the removing action through calls.
A nested each that needs an outer row names it: each(source, key, template, { as: 'order' }), read with row('order.id'). Do not copy outer fields into inner items.
Format numbers, dates and money in derive with Intl, one row per item, and use memoizeItem so one change formats one item (recipe format-values). The grammar has no formatting operators.

title: 5. The view
parts: Write the spec with builders, never by hand:
id is the element's address in the spec; domId is the HTML id. Give anything a test or another agent addresses an explicit, unique id.

each(source, key, template) needs a key that is unique across the whole list and never missing, also in lists built in derive or initialState and in a when branch that is not shown yet. '.' is the key for lists of strings or numbers.
when(condition, children, otherwise) renders only one branch.
A handler is act('namespace.verb', args); a list runs in order, each logged. Keys are 'keydown.Enter' and 'keydown.Control+Shift+k'; options are { preventDefault, stopPropagation }.
Inputs, selects and textareas need aria-label; images need alt; buttons and links need text or a label; no javascript: URL is allowed. The validator checks these at mount.

Dragging is pointer events calling actions. There is no dragstart, drop or dataTransfer; copy recipe drag-reorder, including its keyboard path and Escape. The follow prop needs the plugin withFollow (@ehtb/agent-ui/follow), and rows with transition slide to a new place only with withMoves (@ehtb/agent-ui/moves).

A link is a page load. a({ href: '/about', soft: true }, 'About') makes it faster inside a shell, and route.go does the same from a button; it only works when the target page has the same shell. A swap focuses the page region named by the new title; put domId: 'agent-ui-announcer' and aria-live: 'polite' on a live region in the shell if the site should also announce it politely.
A dialog is a native dialog plus explicit open state; copy recipe modal for the focus trap, focus restore and inert background. The framework has no modal component.

title: 6. Network and plugins
parts: A resources entry belongs to the namespace that declares it, next to its actions:

The lifecycle actions are the only writers of the owned keys, and the response is in the action log, so ui.replay(log) reproduces the state without a network call. Change a watched key to restart the request (a retry flips a flag); onIdle clears owned state when request returns null.

A page rendered on the server already holds its resources' output. By default the browser loads it again on mount; add revalidate: 'never' (with owns) when that output is complete and fresh enough for the first paint, so the first mount trusts the document and a later watched change still loads. Do not combine it with onTimeout: 'serve', whose state may be partial.
Everything else external is a plugin. The ones the package ships (agent-ui explain plugins prints this with the details):
A page lists   From   When
withResources   @ehtb/agent-ui/resources   a namespace declares resources
({ win }) => windowEvents(win, { ... })   @ehtb/agent-ui/window-events   an action answers a window or document event
withHead   @ehtb/agent-ui/head   head is a function of the state
withFollow   @ehtb/agent-ui/follow   the spec uses follow
withMoves   @ehtb/agent-ui/moves   rows with transition should slide when the list reorders
withNavigation (a shell lists it)   @ehtb/agent-ui/navigation   soft links and route.go between the shell's pages
A plugin you write:
It is (environment) => (api) => void, reads with api.watch(keys, callback) and writes with api.dispatch(name, args).
It checks api.replaying before it acts, and registers api.onReplay to drop a request or timer in flight.

The server runs the page's plugins too, against a stand-in window. A plugin with a timer, a window listener, a request or a browser-only library starts with if (isServerRendering) return; (a field of the environment). Copy recipe browser-only-plugin.

To draw into an element (a chart, an editor), call mountElement(api, 'element-id', (element, { key }) => cleanup) from @ehtb/agent-ui/mount-element. The element has an explicit id and no children in the spec; events go back through api.dispatch. Copy recipe draw-into-element.
Never write state from a plugin callback, a binding or an event handler, and never read state from the DOM.

title: 7. Verify
parts: agent-ui check validates every page's finished spec, every literal link and the data the page loads, without a browser. It reports a duplicate or missing list key anywhere in the spec. Run it before you finish.
In a test, use the agent API:
ui.state(), ui.derived(), ui.outline(), ui.tree(), ui.log, ui.errors and ui.replaying are JSON or plain values.
await ui.settle() before asserting on the DOM or outline(). flushAsync(ui) when a fetch is involved.
assertNoErrors(ui) after await ui.settle() and after the step that opens a branch: a list inside a branch the first render did not show is checked at mount only on the data it has then.
assertRepeatable(ui, action, args) on idempotent user actions such as selection, filters and form lookup.

Replay reproduces state from the action log, including the answers resources wrote. It does not replay plugin or DOM side effects (an editor's content, a chart's drawing); test those in a browser with @ehtb/agent-ui/testing/browser.mjs.
Keep a bug as a regression test: record the actions in ui.log and replay them with ui.replay(log).

title: 8. The mistakes that cost the most
parts: A list without a key, a duplicate key, or a key that changes when the item is edited. The row is reused by key.
State mutation in place (items.push(...)) instead of a replacement ([...items, item]).
Writing another namespace directly instead of through calls, or doing fetch/timers inside an action instead of a resource or plugin.
A handler invented on the spot: declare the action and its arguments first.
A literal href that starts with / and is not a page, a file in publicDir or an API path. agent-ui check reports it.

export *, re-exports or default imports/exports in your own files, which the bundler does not support (agent-ui check reports them). Use named imports and relative paths with the extension. A package written with export * (zod, Tiptap) is imported by name and, for the browser, given a one-file esbuild build through replaceModules (BUILD.md, "Vendor files").
Editing dist/ or .agent-ui/: both are generated. Change the source and rebuild.
A session token in state: the state is in the document and reaches the browser. Keep it in an HttpOnly cookie set by the API or a form, and put only public data in initialStateFor.

Forgetting that a page is server-rendered: a plugin with a timer, a listener or a request runs on the server too, against a stand-in window, so guard it with isServerRendering; a library that touches window when it is imported fails on the server, so import it dynamically.

title: 9. What is deliberately not here
parts: No client-side router. Following a link is a page load; soft: true inside a shell makes it faster.
No browser storage. Durable state lives on the server and is loaded with resources.
No component-local state; per-row state is rowState. No scoped CSS.
No virtualization, undo/redo, streaming SSR or partial hydration. A long list is a page of the data at a time; budgets.listRows holds a page to it.

No modal/popover component with a focus trap (copy recipe modal), no file-upload parser or multipart body, and no SSE or WebSocket endpoint. Receive uploads and long-lived connections in the host server.
No built-in internationalization, locale-aware URLs or right-to-left layout. Text and dir are ordinary state and attributes; the project owns the catalogue.

No scroll restoration inside scrolling containers (the window's position is restored on back and forward). A site below a path is basePath in build.config.mjs; write every URL of the site as if it were at the root.
No SVG beyond icons and simple drawings: svg, g, path, circle, ellipse, rect, line, polyline, polygon, use. A chart is a library drawn by a plugin (recipe draw-into-element), no canvas or media tags.
No TypeScript compile step. The package ships hand-written .d.ts files, so // @ts-check gives editor checking without a build; examples/with-typescript is a checked app.

No session store, auth flow or CSP policy. The render server passes the request to initialStateFor, stateForBrowser and transformResponse; keep the session token in an HttpOnly cookie set by the API or a form, and write the policy in your server.

title: Guide
text: Read this before adding or changing a page, a URL or an endpoint. It connects the pieces. If you are an agent, read AGENT-RULES.md in this folder first: it is the short operating manual, and this guide is the map. The exact reference for each piece is in API.md (section 13 for pages) and BUILD.md (the build). The running examples are examples/events (many pages, forms, an API) and examples/shop (code splitting by page) in the framework repository. For a page that does a common thing (a list you edit, a form with validation, an async list, a dialog, a header that stays), start from the recipe: agent-ui explain lists them, agent-ui explain <recipe> prints its files, and the cookbook/ folder of the package holds them as pages that agent-ui check renders.

title: 1. The model
parts: A page is a URL, and a URL is a folder. Every folder below pages/ that holds a page.js is a page, and the folder's path is the page's URL. There is one way to say where a page lives, and nothing else is configured: no list of pages, no entry to name. A site served below a path says so once (basePath in build.config.mjs), and every URL in it is still written as if it were at the root.
Folder   URL
pages/page.js   /
pages/about/page.js   /about
pages/event/archived/page.js   /event/archived
pages/event/[id]/page.js   /event/:id
pages/event/[...path]/page.js   /event/*path

A parameter is written [name] and a rest segment [...name], because : and * are not allowed in file names on every system. The rest segment must be the last folder. A page.js has its content in view.js beside it, and its own helpers (api.js, signup.js, page.css) there too. page.css may @import CSS shared with a few pages; pages/style.css does the same for every page (BUILD.md, "CSS imports"). Anything else in pages/ that is not a page.js is yours (shared modules may live there or in a folder of their own).

Following a link is a page load. There is no client-side router. The links of a page are plain <a href="/about">, the server or the static host answers them with the next page, and the browser app starts again from that page's state. What must outlive a page lives on the server and is loaded with resources: a cart, a profile, the data. Anything kept only in the browser (a typed search text) is gone after a link, by design. A link written soft: true is the same page load made faster, for pages that share a header or a footer that should stay (section 4, "A header that stays, and soft links").
Each page is its own entry in the build, so a page downloads the code it imports and the code pages share, nothing else (BUILD.md, "Pages and chunks").

title: 2. What happens to a URL
parts: Where   What happens

File host (agent-ui build --static)   Every page is rendered at build time and written to <path>/index.html (the page / is index.html). A static site names every page, so a page with parameters is an error.

Render server (agent-ui serve, or createSsrHandler inside your own server)   Every request whose path matches a page's URL pattern is rendered for that URL with the page's own create(). The HTML carries the rendered page and its state. The page's ready(state) says when its data is there, and the server waits for it; after renderTimeoutMs (default 2000) the handler answers 503 rather than serving a half-loaded page with 200. The page's status(state) sets the HTTP status, for example 404 for an unknown id. The handler's initialStateFor, stateForBrowser and transformResponse hooks add public session state, choose what the state script carries, and change an answer's headers or body (section 4, "A session, a CSP and response headers"). A client that disconnects aborts the render; request.signal says so.

Browser   The page starts from the state the server embedded (route.hydrated turns true when it has taken over), reads the URL's parameters into route.params, and runs its resources. A resource declared revalidate: 'never' trusts the server's output on mount instead of loading it a second time (below, "A page that needs data").

When several pages match a path, the most specific wins: compared from the left, a literal segment beats :name, which beats *name. So /event/archived beats /event/:id, which beats /event/*path. Two folders with the same shape, such as [id] and [slug] at the same depth, are an error that names both. A path that matches no page is the host's to answer (404). A path whose last segment has a file extension (/logo.png, /item/v1.2) is treated as a file, never as a page, so a parameter value must not end in . plus letters or digits.

title: A page that needs data
parts: The page declares three things:
Key   Meaning   Example
ready   When the data has arrived. A failure counts as finished, so nothing waits for it.   (state) => state.items.status === 'ready' \ \  state.items.status === 'failed'
pending   What to show until then: a skeleton or "Loading...". A spec; give its elements ids of their own.   p({ id: 'loading' }, 'Loading…')
status   The HTTP status: 404 for an id that names nothing, 503 for a failed load.   (state) => ...
One definition serves everyone:

The render server waits for ready before it renders, so the HTML it sends is the finished page and pending never reaches it. The same goes for a static build (--static), which fails the build if a page never becomes ready.
agent-ui check waits for it too.

In the browser, pending stands in for the page while the resources load in the background. The page replaces it when ready turns true. Every page has the derived value route.ready (true for a page without ready), so a layout can show it.

A page without ready counts as ready at once. A page with ready but no pending shows its view as it is. ready and status read the plain snapshot of state, nested by namespace (state.events.status, state.route.params), not derived names.

A refresh must not undo readiness. By default the browser repeats the resources' requests after the server rendered the page. An onStart action that sets status to 'loading' unconditionally would put a finished page back to pending. Write it as a guard:
(in the loading action of the namespace that owns the data). with-express and examples/loading-states do this.

A resource whose server result is complete and fresh for the first paint can skip that second load: add revalidate: 'never' and list its output keys in owns. The first run on mount then does nothing when the document carries a state script; a later change to a watched key still loads. Do not use it with onTimeout: 'serve' (the state script may be partial), on a resource whose data depends on the visitor in a way the render did not see, or without owns (the definition is refused).

title: Data that belongs to one page
parts: A namespace's resources run for every page that lists the namespace, so list a namespace only on the pages that need it. The checkout page of examples/shop lists cart and checkout but not catalog, so it never requests /products.json.

A resource's output is written only by its lifecycle actions (onStart, onSuccess, onError, onCancel, onIdle); list those keys in owns so dev mode refuses writes from other actions. title: A header that stays, and soft links
parts: A shell is the part of the document that stays while the page inside it is replaced: a header, a footer, a player. It is an app of its own, written like a page in two files, and a link marked soft: true replaces only the page inside it instead of loading a document. Everything else about the link is a normal link: its href is real, and a failed swap, a crawler and a middle click use it.

Write the shell's behavior (defineShell from @ehtb/agent-ui/shell: a name, its own namespaces, plugins: [withNavigation], and what it reads from the page, such as the cart count) and its content ({ name, view }, with pageSlot() where the page goes). examples/shop/shared/shell.js and shell-view.js are the model; API.md, section 13, has the grammar.
In each page that lives in the shell, add shell to page.js and export { shell } (the content) to view.js. The page must have the namespaces the shell reads (the shop's pages all list cart).
Mark the links that should be soft: a({ href: '/checkout', soft: true }, 'Checkout'). For a button, use on: { click: act('route.go', { href: '/checkout' }) }.
Run agent-ui check: it reports a soft link to a page of another shell, or none, and a route.go to a place that is no page.

What the visitor gets is what a page load gives: the URL changes (and back works), the page starts from the state the server rendered for it, its head is the next page's (the description, the attributes of <html> and <body> and the elements it wrote are copied from the document the link fetched; a head that follows the state needs withHead from @ehtb/agent-ui/head), and the page's element takes the focus. The element is a region named by the new title, so a screen reader announces the page when it takes the focus; put domId: 'agent-ui-announcer' on a live region in the shell (domId is the HTML id), usually visually hidden with aria-live: 'polite', if you also want a polite live announcement. What is not carried over is a page's own browser state (a typed search text). A shell stays mounted, so its state stays; keep in it only what the shell shows. Anything that is not a plain page (a 404, a redirect, a page of another shell) is a normal page load, with the reason in the console.

title: A session, a CSP and response headers
parts: createSsrHandler reads each request once into { method, pathname, search, query, headers, cookies, signal } and gives the request to the page's render, api.handle, api.handleForm, initialStateFor, stateForBrowser, transformResponse and the page's data requests (fetchFunction(url, init, request)). For a rendered form outcome, the page render, initialStateFor, stateForBrowser, transformResponse, its resources and data requests read the outcome page's path and query with the POST's method, headers and cookies (section 12). The framework has no session store, login flow, authorization or CSP policy. It gives you the request and three hooks; the policy is yours:

A session token belongs in an HttpOnly cookie, set by the API or a form handler that changes the session. A page cannot set response headers; an API, a form outcome and transformResponse can set a cookie. Check the cookie, the Origin header or a CSRF token in the handler that changes state.

To protect a page, return the public session state in initialStateFor and answer status(state) 403 when state.session.user is null; render a sign-in prompt, not the protected content, and keep initialStateFor public. A page cannot set a redirect header. The API and form handlers must check the session too: a page status protects the page, not the data.

request.cookies holds raw values, not percent-decoded; request.query is a URLSearchParams; request.headers are Node's lower-case names. request.signal aborts when the client disconnects; the render already passes it to resources and their data requests, and a host query should take it too.

A page that never becomes ready answers 503 after renderTimeoutMs (default 2000, or timeoutMs on the handler); onTimeout: 'serve' is the explicit option that sends the partial page instead. The handler reads JSON and URL-encoded bodies up to maxBodyBytes (default 100 KB) and answers 415 for another content type, including multipart/form-data; receive an upload in a host route and pass the parsed value as request.body.

initialStateFor returns public state in the shape of ui.state(); every key must be declared by the page. If it returns a session namespace on every request, import one shared session namespace into every page. It is not a place to authorize: the page only renders what it is given. A shell is an app of its own and does not receive this state: if the shell shows the visitor, have the page declare the namespace and the shell reads the key (API.md section 13, "Shell and soft navigation").

stateForBrowser(state, request) returns the state the document's state script carries after the page rendered. Keep the page's namespaces and keys and leave a server-only one out; it cannot add a key, because the browser app would not have it declared. It is a serialization boundary, not a secret store: the markup was rendered from the full state, and a value in the page's declared default is in the browser bundle. Put server-only data in initialStateFor with a neutral declared default and remove it here. During a static build and agent-ui check the request is null.

transformResponse(request, { status, headers, body }) runs after the framework's content type and cache default and the API's or form outcome's headers. Return { headers?, body? } or null. Return only headers to add or replace: the headers passed in contain the framework's own headers (for example content-type on a page or API answer) and its security header, and those names are refused in a returned object, so read them and do not spread them. A returned header replaces the existing one; set-cookie values add up; the framework's security header is merged last. A returned body must be the whole body as a string. The body may be HTML, JSON or plain text: check headers['content-type'] before rewriting it.

A nonce needs both a header and a body rewrite, which is why it is one hook: the example adds the same nonce to the CSP and to every inline script. The page's module script is external and covered by 'self'; the state-script reader and soft navigation accept attributes in any order, so the added nonce does not break hydration or a soft link. A page's CSS is an external stylesheet covered by style-src 'self'; a page that emits inline style needs a hash, a nonce or 'unsafe-inline', which the host decides. A soft navigation copies the next page's head and body scripts; an inline script that differs is created and runs, but the fetched document's nonce belongs to that response, not to the CSP of the document that stays. Keep page behavior in its module entry or a plugin when a soft link is used; do not rely on an inline script there. The state script is data, not code.

The hook runs for every answer this handler writes once a request context exists, including its 404 and 500 and the 400 for a body it cannot read, but not for a request that goes to next() or for the 421 and 400 answered before a request context exists. If it throws, the visitor gets a 500 and the hook is not run again on that answer.

A page cannot set response headers. transformResponse sets a page's cache policy or CSP; set a site policy unconditionally in the transform to make it a floor. A page whose state depends on the visitor should have the host send vary: cookie or cache-control: private from transformResponse for every answer: no-cache alone does not separate visitors in a shared cache.

fetchFunction(url, init, request) can forward the visitor's cookie or authorization header to your data source. prerender and agent-ui check have no request, so the third argument is undefined there: a page whose data depends on the visitor cannot be statically generated.

A host server or plugin that writes its own response can use checkResponseHeaders and mergeResponseHeaders from @ehtb/agent-ui/http-headers, so its headers follow the same checks and merge order (API.md section 12).

title: 5. What is not automatic
parts: A session store, a login flow, authorization and a CSP policy are the project's. The framework passes the request and applies what the hooks return; it does not write a nonce, choose a policy, or decide who may see a page (section 4, "A session, a CSP and response headers").
There is no streaming render and no partial hydration: the server sends one document after the page is ready (or a 503 by default), and the whole state script is the handover.

There is no file-upload parser, no streaming request body, no SSE endpoint and no WebSocket endpoint. Receive those in the host server; pass a parsed body to the API as request.body, or serve the connection beside the handler.

A modal, menu or popover is not a component with a focus trap. Use a native dialog with explicit state and copy recipe modal: its plugin traps the focus, restores it on close and marks the background inert.
Translation, locale-aware URLs and right-to-left direction are the project's. Text and dir are ordinary state and attributes; the framework ships no message catalogue.

A static site (agent-ui build --static) writes every page, and a page with parameters once for every URL its view.js lists in export const paths = [...] (or an async function); a page with parameters that lists none, or a status other than 200, stops the build with the reason. agent-ui check renders the same URLs and prints a note for a page with parameters that lists none.
The API is Node code. A file host has no API: the static pages and the browser app work, but calls to /api/... and plain form posts do not.

A site below a path of its domain is basePath: '/shop' in build.config.mjs (BUILD.md, "A site below a base path"). Specs, folders, resources and the API keep writing the site's own paths; a url() in CSS is relative to the stylesheet.
Code splitting is by page: everything a page lists is in its chunk. A heavy feature inside one page is a plain import() (a lazy chunk).

Soft navigation does not prefetch the next page; back and forward restore the window's scroll position, not the one inside a scrolling container; a page's own browser state does not survive a swap, as it does not survive a load.
The forms handler and the form element's action are matched by you. The tests in examples/events/app.test.mjs post to both to catch drift.
text: A session store, a login flow, authorization and a CSP policy are the project's. The framework passes the request and applies what the hooks return; it does not write a nonce, choose a policy, or decide who may see a page (section 4, "A session, a CSP and response headers"). There is no streaming render and no partial hydration: the server sends one document after the page is ready (or a 503 by default), and the whole state script is the handover. There is no file-upload parser, no streaming request body, no SSE endpoint and no WebSocket endpoint. Receive those in the host server; pass a parsed body to the API as request.body, or serve the connection beside the handler. A modal, menu or popover is not a component with a focus trap. Use a native dialog with explicit state and copy recipe modal: its plugin traps the focus, restores it on close and marks the background inert. Translation, locale-aware URLs and right-to-left direction are the project's. Text and dir are ordinary state and attributes; the framework ships no message catalogue. title: 5a. Reporting errors (Sentry and the like)
parts: A production build keeps no sentences: an error is a code and its details (AUI0202 {"action":"todos.add"}, and error.code, error.details), which is also what a monitoring tool groups by. Register a plugin that hands the errors the runtime catches (a failed dispatch, a blocked URL, an update that threw) to the tool; the action log is a repro you can send with them, because replay reproduces the state from it.
The log holds the arguments of the actions. If they can hold personal data, send the action names (api.log.slice(-20).map(([name]) => name)) or filter the arguments first.

Decode on the server side, not in the page: import { decodeError } from '@ehtb/agent-ui/error-messages' in a script that reads your issues, or in a beforeSend that runs in Node (decodeError(error).text is the sentence the development build would have said). Source maps (agent-ui build --source-maps) restore the stack the same way. In the browser nothing of the catalogue is downloaded.
agent-ui explain 'AUI0103 {"operation":"get","key":"todos.drat"}' decodes one by hand. The codes and their details are listed in docs/API.md, section 9.
Errors that are thrown out of the page (the app cannot start) are not caught by onError: they reach window.onerror, which the tool already hooks.

title: 6. When it does not work
parts: Symptom   Likely cause   Fix
page "/x": unknown key "vew"   misspelled key in a page   use the suggested key; the message lists the allowed ones
pages/a/page.js: its URL "/a/:slug" matches the same URLs as "/a/:id"   two parameter folders at the same depth   merge the pages, or give one a fixed segment
the folder name "x y" cannot be part of a URL   a folder with a space or other character   letters, digits and . _ ~ - for a fixed segment, [name] for a parameter
"[...path]" must be the last folder of the path   a page below a catch-all folder   move the catch-all to the end

agent-ui check prints /x/*rest has parameters and its view.js lists no \`paths\`   a page with parameters has no URL of its own to render   its spec is still validated; to render it, export paths = ['/x/a/b'] from its view.js (the same URLs --static writes)
the link "/chekout" is no page   a typo in an href   the message suggests the nearest page
the soft link "/x" is on a page without a shell   soft on a page that has no shell: nothing handles it   give the page a shell, or remove soft
the soft link "/x" leads to /x, which has no shell   a soft link to a page that is not in this page's shell   give both pages the shell, or remove soft
page "/": page.js names the shell "main", but view.js exports no shell   the behavior is in page.js and the content is missing from view.js (or the reverse)   export shell from both
shell "main" reads[0]: watch key "cart.count" is not a state key ...   the page lacks a namespace the shell reads   list that namespace in the page's namespaces
soft navigation to /x: ... Loading it as a normal page in the console   the answer was not a plain page, or a page of another shell   the link still works as a page load; read the reason it names
A URL shows the host's 404   no page matches it   add a folder, or a [...path] page for a not-found page
namespace "x": declares resources, but no plugin loads them   the page lacks plugins: [withResources]   add it
derived "events.visible": get("search.query"): there is no namespace "search"   a namespace reads another that the page does not list   list it in the page's namespaces
/api/... returns No such endpoint.   the table's name differs from the URL, or the pattern does not match   endpoints live at /api/<name> plus the pattern
/api/... returns 405 with an allow header   the path matches an endpoint, but not for this method   use a method from allow, or add 'METHOD /pattern' to the table's endpoints
form "/x": outcome url "..." is not allowed   a forms handler returned a url that is not a local path   return a path starting with / and not //, for example url: '/contact'
A form post renders the default page   initialState lacks a state key the outcome sets   include it, nested by namespace

The page shows "loading" in the HTML   the page's ready never became true, or the data URL is not answered at render time   check that fetchFunction in build.config.mjs (a host that answers from its own process puts its function in the config it passes to createSsrHandler) answers that URL; agent-ui check names the page
ready(state) returned ... not true or false   ready returned something else   return a boolean
Production build misses a check you saw in development   the spec validator is left out of production builds   run agent-ui check or build with --dev

title: API reference
text: This file is authoritative for everything under src/. If code and this file disagree, fix one of them in the same change. Everything here is implemented and tested unless marked proposed. Bundling and shipping an app is in BUILD.md. The reasons behind the design are in DESIGN.md. Contents: 1 mental model, 2 a complete minimal app, 3 spec grammar, 4 namespaces: state, derive, actions, 5 update model, 6 plugins, 7 agent API, 8 spec tools, 9 validator and error catalogue, 10 testing, 11 recipes, 12 components, reusable namespaces, server rendering, types and dev loop, 13 pages, 14 limits.

title: 1. Mental model
parts: An app is two values:

namespaces: { name: { state, derive, actions, resources, shapes, rowState } }. state is the initial data as JSON, derive holds pure functions computed from state, and actions are named, typed functions, the only code that writes state. Every state key, derived value and action belongs to exactly one namespace and writes only its own (section 4).
spec: the UI tree, as data.

Nothing else carries behavior. Anything that touches the outside world (network, timers, window events) is a plugin. A plugin talks to the app only through api.watch (state out) and api.dispatch (changes in), so every change of state is an action in the log.

app validates the namespaces and the spec first and throws an Error that lists the problems one per line (error.problems is the list) when it finds any. debug: true makes the browser console show what the app does (the debug console, below); debug is false unless you say otherwise. It then creates one signal per state key, renders into root, runs the plugins, and returns the agent API (section 7). initialState (optional) is a partial state in the shape of ui.state(), { namespace: { key: value } }, laid over the declared state; it is how server-rendered state arrives. An unknown namespace or key in it is an error with a suggestion. dev is required, true or false, with no default: true deep-freezes state so an in-place mutation fails loudly and turns the development checks on, false is for production. A generated browser entry writes it down (true in a development build), so the mode is never guessed.

The grammar is machine-readable: import { grammar } from '@ehtb/agent-ui' gives the allowed tags, events, key modifiers, binding keys, argument types and node keys. These are the same constants the validator uses.

title: Importing
parts: The package is imported by name. Every module has one specifier, types included. The bundler resolves these the way Node does, through the package's exports.
Import   What it is
@ehtb/agent-ui   the runtime: app, signal, effect, settle, validate, grammar, mergeInitialState, countEffectRuns
@ehtb/agent-ui/head   the plugin withHead, which keeps the browser's document current as the state changes, for a page whose head is a function of the state (section 13, "Head")
@ehtb/agent-ui/resources, /window-events, /follow, /moves   plugins; a page downloads only the ones it imports. All the plugins, and when to list each: section 6, "The plugins the package ships"
@ehtb/agent-ui/spec   the builders (section 3, "Builders"): div(...), state(...), act(...), each, when, one function per tag and operator
@ehtb/agent-ui/mount-element   mountElement(api, id, mount): how a plugin that draws into an element (a chart, an editor, a map) claims it (section 6, "Plugins that draw into an element")

@ehtb/agent-ui/spec-tools, /components, /memoize, /sync-apps   patchSpec, listIds, expandComponents, defineElement, param, paramKey, slot, memoizeItem, syncApps (one-way sync between two separate apps on a page, section 6)

@ehtb/agent-ui/shell, /navigation   defineShell (the part of a document that stays while the page changes) and the plugin withNavigation (soft links and route.go): section 13, "Shell and soft navigation"
@ehtb/agent-ui/pages, /url-pattern   definePage and startPage (section 13), and compileUrlPattern / sortBySpecificity, the URL patterns that pages and API tables share
@ehtb/agent-ui/messages   fail(where, problem, fix) and didYouMean(word, candidates): the one shape of every error, for plugins and project code that follow rule 12

@ehtb/agent-ui/http-headers   checkResponseHeaders(headers, where, options) and mergeResponseHeaders(...layers): the checks and merge order the render handler applies to API, form and transform headers; for a host server or plugin that writes its own response (section 12, "Request context, response headers and a session")
@ehtb/agent-ui/server, /hydrate   server rendering (renderPage) and the browser side (browserEnvironment)

@ehtb/agent-ui/server/ssr-handler.mjs   createSsrHandler: a request handler (request, response, next?) for your own Node server that renders the pages and handles the api module; it serves no files. Its initialStateFor, stateForBrowser and transformResponse hooks add public state, choose what the document carries, and change an answer's headers or body (section 12)
@ehtb/agent-ui/spec-schema   createSpecSchema(): the JSON Schema of the spec
@ehtb/agent-ui/devtools   the debug console (mountDevtools): what the app does, written to the browser console

@ehtb/agent-ui/cli/ssr-server.mjs, /cli/static-handler.mjs   createSsrServer, createStaticServer: the servers behind agent-ui serve and agent-ui dev, for tests and examples. Not for production: a deployed site is served by the host's own file server
@ehtb/agent-ui/build   the build pipeline as a library (Node only): build, loadConfig, frameworkBuildOptions, prerender (the static build), discoverPages, formatReport

@ehtb/agent-ui/build/build.mjs, /build/config.mjs, /build/prerender.mjs   one stage of the build pipeline, the configuration loader and the static build, for a script that drives a build itself (Node only)

title: 3. Spec grammar
parts: An unknown key anywhere in a node is a validation error. chilren is reported with a suggestion, never ignored.
text: An unknown key anywhere in a node is a validation error. chilren is reported with a suggestion, never ignored.

title: Bindings
parts: Binding   Value

{state: "todos.draft"}   The state key or derived value draft of the namespace todos, then any optional-chained path inside its value: {state: "todos.current.title"} is key todos.current, path .title. Always written with its namespace. Re-evaluated when that key changes.

{item: "field"}   Field of the current row's item. Valid inside an each template, including nested when and each. In a nested each, {item} is the innermost row. {item: "."} is the item itself, for lists of strings or numbers.

{row: "name.field"}   Field of the item of an enclosing each that said as: "name", from any depth below it. {row: "name"} is that whole item (lists of strings or numbers). Also valid as a handler argument. See "each".

{rowState: "namespace.field"} or {rowState: "rowname.namespace.field"}   The value of field in the rowState of namespace, for the row of the innermost each (the row key is the each's key), or, with three parts, for the row of the enclosing each that said as: "rowname". See "Per-row state".
{not: x}   !x.
{length: x}   x.length, or 0 for null and undefined. Works for arrays and strings.

{equals: [x, y]}   x === y: strict equality, so two lists or objects are equal only when they are the same value (the same reference), even when their contents match. Compare strings, numbers and booleans, or a field of them ({item: 'id'}). A derived value, by contrast, keeps its previous reference when a recompute is structurally equal to it, to depth 2 (isSameValue), so rows do not re-render for nothing; that rule is about what re-renders, not about equals.
{greaterThan: [x, y]}, {lessThan: [x, y]}   > and <.
{and: [...]}, {or: [...]}   Boolean every and some over truthiness, at least 2 operands. They return true or false, not an operand.
{join: [...]}   Concatenates operands as strings; null and undefined become empty. Use it to build text, class strings, URLs and style strings from several values.

As a child, a binding renders text. null and undefined become empty; numbers and booleans are stringified. Operands are bindings or literals (string, number, boolean, null). An object operand that is not a binding is an error.

title: Elements
parts: Field   Meaning

tag   One of the allowed tags, listed in grammar.tags: div span p h1 h2 h3 ul ol li button input label a section header footer main nav form select option textarea strong em b i small code pre blockquote hr br img table thead tbody tfoot tr th td caption dl dt dd details summary dialog aside article fieldset legend figure figcaption progress time, and the SVG tags svg g path circle ellipse rect line polyline polygon use (see "SVG"). Void tags (input, img, hr, br, and the SVG shapes) cannot have children.

id   Stable address, rendered as data-id. Must be a unique non-empty string within the spec. Defaults to the spec path (see "Default ids"). Give an explicit id to anything tests or other agents must find across edits.
props   {name: literal \  binding}. See "Props" below.

classes   {className: binding}. Values must be bindings, never true or false literals; constant classes go in props.class. The final class attribute is the static props.class plus every class whose binding is truthy, written as one attribute and removed when empty.
on   { "event": handler }. See "Events and handlers".
transition   A positive number of milliseconds. See "Transitions".
children   A node or an array of nodes.

Props. value, checked and disabled are DOM properties, written only when they differ from the current value. focus: true calls element.focus() after insertion. follow (a boolean or a boolean binding, never an attribute) makes the element track the pointer while it is true: see "Following the pointer". soft: true on a link (a with an href; a literal, never a binding) makes following it a soft navigation when the page has a shell that listens: it is written as the attribute data-soft, and everything else about the link stays a normal link (section 13, "Shell and soft navigation"). Every other name is an attribute: true sets an empty attribute, false and null remove it. For aria-* names, booleans become the strings "true" and "false", and false does not remove them. data-agent-ui-* names are the framework's (they mark what a server wrote into the head) and are refused in a view.

Order is handled for you. type is applied before the other props, and a select's value is applied after its options exist. A select's value is not re-applied when its options change later; re-select by binding value to state that changes.
The validator reports names from other conventions at mount: className, htmlFor and onClick-style names. It also reports object values (style must be a string; build it with join) and unsafe URLs.

URL safety. Values of href, src, action and formaction that start with javascript: or vbscript: are blocked: the attribute is removed and errors records it. data: is blocked everywhere except the src of an element that shows it (an img); the src of a <script> in the head is checked like an href. Literal violations are reported by the validator, bound ones at runtime.

Transitions. After the first render, a row of an each or a branch of a when whose root element has transition gets data-transition="enter" for two frames when it is added. When it is removed it gets data-transition="leave" for that many milliseconds first, and ignores events meanwhile. CSS does the animating, for example li { transition: opacity .2s } [data-transition] { opacity: 0 }. State is final immediately; only the DOM removal is delayed. Initial and server-rendered markup never animates.

Moves. With the plugin withMoves (@ehtb/agent-ui/moves; moves for app()), a row of a keyed each whose root element has transition also slides when it changes position: before the reorder the plugin measures the row (getBoundingClientRect), after it plays element.animate from the old spot to the new one (a translate, FLIP) for that many milliseconds. Nothing else is needed in the spec or the CSS, and only the rows that moved are animated. Without the plugin the rows jump to their places, and in development the runtime says so in the console, once per list, with the import. It is skipped, and the row simply jumps, where there is no layout or no Element.animate (server rendering, the test shim), while ui.replaying, and when the user prefers reduced motion. The animation sets transform for its length, so do not rely on a transform of your own on such a row.

Following the pointer. follow: <boolean binding> in props (the drag overlay of a sortable list, a slider thumb). The plugin withFollow (@ehtb/agent-ui/follow; follow for app()) does the following; a spec that uses follow without it fails at mount with that import in the message. While it is true the plugin listens to pointermove on the document, and only for that time. On every frame it writes --follow-x and --follow-y (for example 37px) on the element: how far the element must move from the place its layout gave it, so that it stays under the pointer where it was grabbed. The first move after follow turns true fixes the start. The CSS decides what to do with them: [data-dragging] { transform: translate(var(--follow-x, 0px), var(--follow-y, 0px)); pointer-events: none }. The coordinates are not state and not in the log, so replay and tests are unaffected, and nothing runs while follow is false. When a keyed each reorders its rows, the following row is re-placed at once, and it is not part of the "Moves" animation. Give a following row pointer-events: none, or the rows beneath it never receive pointerover. Touch: the pointer is captured by the element that received pointerdown, and its moves still reach the document, so the element follows. The properties are removed when follow turns false, and nothing is written after that. follow follows whatever binds it, not how the drag began: a state that is true after a keyboard pick-up makes the element follow the mouse too. If a page ends the drag with a handler on a broad ancestor (a pointerup on main), every pointer release there is a logged action, a no-op when nothing is being dragged. A literal other than true/false is refused by the validator.

Drag and drop. The grammar has no dragstart, dragover, drop or dataTransfer, and none will be added: a drag is the bubbling pointer events (pointerdown on a grip, pointerover on the rows it crosses, pointerup and pointercancel) calling actions, with follow for the picked-up row and transition for the others (the page lists their plugins, withFollow and withMoves). A touch pointer is captured by the grip and never reports the rows it crosses, so the keyboard (Enter, the arrow keys, Escape) is both the touch path and the accessible one, and belongs in every sortable list. Copy the recipe drag-reorder (agent-ui explain drag-reorder, tested in test/examples/cookbook.test.mjs); examples/react-converted-components builds a reusable sortable on the same pattern.

SVG. A closed subset for icons and simple drawings: svg, g, path, circle, ellipse, rect, line, polyline, polygon, use (grammar.svgTags). The runtime makes them in the SVG namespace; on the server they are markup, which an HTML parser puts in that namespace by itself. Their attributes are grammar.svgAttributes (viewBox, fill, stroke, stroke-width, d, cx, points, transform, ...) besides href, width, height, class, style and the global ones; an SVG attribute on an HTML tag is refused. The rules, all checked by the validator: a shape (every SVG tag but svg) stands only inside an svg; an svg holds only SVG tags, no text and no HTML; an svg either says what it shows (role: 'img' with an aria-label) or is 'aria-hidden': 'true' beside text that says it. An icon used many times comes from a sprite in public/ (use({ href: '/icons.svg#star' }), the base path added like any URL). What is drawn from data (the points of a line) is a derived value. A large or interactive chart is a library drawn by a plugin (mountElement). Copy recipe svg-icons.

title: Events and handlers
parts: A handler is [actionName, args?, options?], where actionName is namespace.verb ('todos.add'). An event may also have a list of handlers, [['todos.add', {...}], ['draft.clear']]: they run in order, each as its own logged action, and every argument is read before the first one runs (so {state} arguments see the state as it was when the event happened). The first action that fails stops the list. For preventDefault, the handlers that state it decide (any true prevents; false everywhere opts out); if none states it, a submit is prevented as usual. A list has at least two handlers (a list of one is the handler itself).

Events: click, dblclick, pointerdown, pointermove, pointerup, pointercancel, pointerover, pointerout, input, change, keydown, keyup, focusin, focusout, submit. They are delegated from the mount root. The nearest element with a matching handler, walking up from the target, fires. Handlers on its ancestors do not also fire. The pointer events are the bubbling ones (mouse, touch and pen); pointerenter and pointerleave do not bubble, so they are not here. {event: "pointerType"} reads "mouse", "touch" or "pen".

Keys: keydown.Enter, keyup.Escape, keydown.Control+Shift+k. The chord is the modifiers present, in the fixed order Control+Alt+Shift+Meta, then event.key as the browser reports it, so a shifted ? is Shift+?. An exact chord handler wins over a plain keydown handler on the same element. keydown.Enter does not fire while Shift is held; the plain keydown handler, if any, fires instead.

args: {argument: value}. A value is a literal, {state: path} (read at event time), {item: field} (the row item at event time), {row: name.field} (a field of an enclosing named row), or {event: "target.value"} (a path into the event; use target.checked for checkboxes). The set of argument names must match the action's declaration exactly. Literal types are checked statically. A json literal may be an object or array; an object is read as a binding when it has a top-level state, item, row or rowState key (or is {event}), so do not use those keys in literal data, and the builder and validator refuse an object with an operator key (not, length, equals, greaterThan, lessThan, and, or, join).

options: {preventDefault?: boolean, stopPropagation?: boolean}. submit handlers call preventDefault by default, because a form submits to an action, not to a server. Pass {preventDefault: false} to opt out. Other events keep their default unless asked.

title: each
parts: each names a state or derived key ("todos.visible"), or is a binding such as {item: "tags"} for nested lists. key names a field that is unique per item, or is "." when the item itself is the key. The template is exactly one element.

Reading the outer row. {item} is always the innermost row. When an inner template needs a field of an outer row (an order's id for a line's remove button, a customer's name for a line's label), the outer each gives its row a name with as, and anything inside it, at any depth, reads it with {row: "name.field"}, in bindings and in handler arguments:

The name is an identifier (letters and digits, starting with a lowercase letter) and cannot repeat the name of an enclosing each (the inner one would hide the outer). {row} follows the outer row when its item is replaced, and the validator checks it when the mount happens: a row outside any as fails with the names in scope and "Did you mean", and when the outer list has a shape (shapes) the field is checked against it. The recipe is nested-rows (agent-ui explain nested-rows). There is no need to copy outer fields into the inner items in derive.

Rows are created once per key and reused. A row's {item} bindings re-run only when the item reference changed. Rows are reordered in place, and a removed row has its effects disposed. Each row's root element gets data-key. An item without a usable key (missing, null, or an object) is reported in errors and skipped. A duplicate key is reported, with the list's source and the positions of the two items. In development the lists that read a state or derived key are also checked when the app mounts, including those inside a when branch that is not shown yet, so a duplicate in the data is found before the branch opens (agent-ui check reports it); a list below another each is checked when a row renders. The check at mount is development-only; a list that renders reports the duplicate as AUI0303 in production too, and the list skips the later item.

title: when
parts: Renders children while the binding is truthy and otherwise while it is falsy. At least one of the two is required. Only the active branch exists. It is rebuilt when truthiness flips, not on every change, and the other branch's effects are disposed.

title: Builders (src/spec.js)
parts: Builders are how a spec is written; the JSON above is what they produce (the wire format the validator, the server renderer, the browser and the action log see). Write builders: a wrong call fails at its own line with the builder's name and the fix, and the shape is the one models have seen most (an element is a tag name, attributes and children). @ehtb/agent-ui/spec writes the same JSON as function calls, and a wrong call fails at the line that made it, with the builder's name and the fix. A builder returns exactly the object you would have written by hand (a test compares them), so the validator, patchSpec, server rendering and the action log see no difference, and raw JSON and builders can be mixed in one spec.
Builder   Result

tag(attributes \  null, ...children) for every tag in the grammar   { tag, props, children }. id, classes, on, transition keep their meaning; every other attribute is a prop. domId is the HTML id attribute (props.id), because id is the element's address in the spec. Children may be text, bindings, elements, each, when, components, or arrays of them (flattened one level). The first argument is always the attributes object or null.

state(path), item(path), row(path), rowState(path), event(path)   { state: path }, { item: path }, { row: path }, { rowState: path }, { event: path } (event only as a handler argument). state paths are namespace.key, then any path inside the value; a path without a namespace fails at the call.
not, length, equals, greaterThan, lessThan, and, or, join   The operators, with the operand counts of the grammar.
act(name, args?, options?)   A handler [name, args?, options?]; name is namespace.verb. The on values must be made with it, or be a list of them.
when(condition, children, otherwise?), each(source, key, template, { as }?)   when and each nodes. { as: 'name' } names the row for row('name.field') in the template.

Mistakes caught at the call: a plain string as the first argument (div('text')), another framework's names (className, htmlFor, onClick, props, children), an unknown event or handler option (with "Did you mean"), classes values that are not bindings, a number or null as a child, children on a void tag, a wrong operand count, a when with nothing to show, an each template that is not one element. Production builds replace the checking module with a stub (replaceModules, as for the validator), so a builder there is only an object constructor. The validator still checks the finished spec as a whole (state keys, action names and arguments, ids, accessibility).

title: Default ids
parts: The root is 0. Child i of an element at path p is p.i. Branch children are p.when.i and p.otherwise.i. An each template is p.each. A when or each node counts as one child of its parent. Paths shift when siblings are added, so use explicit ids for anything you address.

title: 4. Namespaces: state, derive, actions
parts: A namespace is { state?, derive?, actions?, resources?, shapes?, rowState? }, and namespaces is { name: namespace }. Every state key, derived value and action belongs to exactly one namespace.

Names. Namespace names, state keys, derived names and action verbs are identifiers: letters and digits, starting with a lowercase letter (todos, nextId, setDraft). No dots and no dashes: the dot separates the parts of a qualified name. The qualified forms are the only forms outside the code of a namespace:
Where   Written
a state binding, an each source, an action argument {state}, a watch list of a plugin, ui.get(...)   todos.draft (state key or derived value), then any path inside the value: todos.current.title
an action in a handler, dispatch, the log, windowEvents, calls   todos.add
ui.state(), ui.derived(), initialState   { todos: { items, draft } }, nested by namespace

Inside a namespace. An action's store and a derived value's get are scoped. A key of the namespace itself is written plain (store.get('draft'), get('items')); a key of any other namespace is written with its namespace (get('search.query')), for reading only. One form for each: writing store.get('todos.draft') inside todos is an error that says to drop the namespace.

An action writes only its own namespace. store.set('search.query', ...) from a todos action fails with state key "search.query" belongs to namespace "search", and todos.add belongs to "todos". An action writes only its own namespace. If this change follows from todos.add, list one of the actions of "search" in calls and use call(...) (search.clear); if it does not, the state is in the wrong namespace: move it, or derive it. Ownership is checked in production builds too, because it is how the scoped store resolves keys.

Design rule: derive or move first. Most cross-namespace writes are a sign that state sits in the wrong namespace, or that the second value is derivable from the first. Reach for calls for a real workflow: one user action whose consequence belongs to another concern ("add the todo, then clear the search box").

title: state
parts: state is a JSON-serializable object. Each key becomes one signal (named namespace.key), and a write replaces the whole key. Values are immutable, and frozen in dev mode.

Every value must survive JSON.stringify unchanged. A function, undefined, NaN, a Date, a Map, a Set, a class instance or a loop is refused at mount. The message gives the path and what to store instead, for example state todos.rows[1].at: undefined is not JSON. Use null for "no value".
