title: Loading and status per page
parts: ready(state) is the one definition of "this page has its data". renderPage, the static build, agent-ui check and the SSR handler wait for it. pending replaces the page content until it is true, through the derived value route.ready that the page's spec binds to.

status(state) sets the HTTP status, read through ui.getStatus(). A page GET is cache-control: no-cache; transformResponse can set a cache policy. A page cannot set response headers: the API, a form outcome and transformResponse can, and transformResponse runs after the framework's headers, so a host can enforce a site policy (section 12, "The request context, response headers and a session").

Both receive the snapshot of all state, { namespace: { key: value } } (the same state that head receives, and the URL's parameters are state.route.params), and are checked when they run: ready must return a boolean (checked as soon as the page starts) and status a whole number from 100 to 599. The message names the page. agent-ui check calls ui.getStatus(), so a bad status is found without a request.

To protect a page, return the public session state in initialStateFor and answer status(state) 403 when state.session.user is null; render a sign-in prompt, not the protected content, and keep initialStateFor public. A page cannot set a redirect header. The API and form handlers must check the session too: a page status protects the page, not the data.

title: Static generation
parts: agent-ui build --static also renders every page and writes it to <path>/index.html (the page / to index.html), so a file host can serve finished pages with no server. A page whose path has parameters (/event/:id, /docs/*path) is written once for every URL its view.js lists:

view.js runs only in Node, so a function may read files or a database and never reaches a browser. Each URL must match the page's pattern, be plain (letters, digits and . _ ~ - in its segments, no query, no trailing slash) and appear once; a page without parameters has no paths. A page with parameters that lists none stops a static build with an error that names the pages and the fix. Without --static nothing is rendered at build time, and agent-ui serve renders every URL per request.
agent-ui check renders the same URLs: every page without parameters, and a page with parameters at its paths. One that lists none is printed as a note, and its spec is still validated.

title: Per-page API
parts: api.js next to the page's page.js exports a table. composeApi (the project's own file, examples/events/compose-api.js: copy it and change it; the framework only asks for the api object it returns, see docs/BUILD.md) mounts endpoints below <apiBase>/<name>/ (apiBase is an option of composeApi, default '/api', no trailing slash) and the forms at the page paths:

handle and handleForm receive the same request context as the page (method, pathname, search, query, headers, cookies, signal), plus body or form. See section 12 for the shape and for initialStateFor, stateForBrowser and transformResponse.
A table cannot answer another table's paths. An unknown path below apiBase is a 404 JSON answer. A path that exists for other methods is a 405 with an allow header.

An endpoint returns { status, body, headers? }, or { status, body, headers?, raw: true } when the body is already the exact bytes to send (CSV, XML, a file). A JSON answer is sent as JSON with application/json; charset=utf-8. A raw answer must be a string or a Uint8Array and must set its own content-type unless the body is empty. A string raw body may be rewritten by transformResponse; a Uint8Array is sent unchanged, its hook receives an empty body, and returning a body for it is refused. An API answer is cache-control: no-store unless the endpoint or transformResponse sets one, and it may set a cookie; the header rules are the ones in section 12.

The handler reads a request body only as JSON (application/json, including application/*+json) or a URL-encoded form (application/x-www-form-urlencoded), with the maxBodyBytes limit (default 100 KB). A body with no content type, multipart/form-data or another type, and a compressed body (any content-encoding but identity), is answered 415; a body over maxBodyBytes is answered 413 (a declared content-length before reading, a chunked body while it is read); a body it cannot parse is answered 400. Decoding a compressed body is the host's: its body parser decodes it and passes the value as request.body. An empty body is accepted as {}. A host framework that parses the body itself can put the parsed value on request.body, which the handler uses as it is. Multipart uploads, streaming request bodies, SSE and WebSocket endpoints are not part of this handler; receive an upload in a route of the host and pass the parsed value as request.body.

A form handler returns the outcome as initialState, nested by namespace; the URL's parameters are filled in for you, so the plain HTML form works without JavaScript. url is the page that shows the outcome: a local path starting with /, not //, with no backslash or encoded separator at the start. A form may instead answer { redirect } under the same rule. redirect is answered with 303 (post/redirect/get), so a reload does not post again. Both outcomes may carry headers.

The framework sets cache-control: no-store on a form response; its headers cannot set location or cache-control, and transformResponse can replace the framework's cache header, but a form response must not be made cacheable.
The browser side of the same feature is a resources entry in the page's namespace. Keep the validation rules in one pure module imported by both.
To give one URL under a parameter page its own page, add a folder next to it (pages/item/archived/page.js). It wins for that URL, and the parameter page keeps the rest.

A path that exists for other methods is a 405 with an allow header. An endpoint returns { status, body, headers? }, or { status, body, headers?, raw: true } when the body is already the exact bytes to send (CSV, XML, a file). A JSON answer is sent as JSON with application/json; charset=utf-8. A raw answer must be a string or a Uint8Array and must set its own content-type unless the body is empty. title: Head
parts: head in page.js is everything the page says about the document around its app. Every value may be a literal or a function of the state snapshot (the same state as in ready and status).
An element is { tag, props, children }, as in the spec. A prop that is false, null or undefined is left out and true writes the attribute bare (defer).

The server writes it while it renders. describePage(state) returns the resolved description ({ title, description, html, body, tags, bodyTags }), and the build and createSsrHandler write it into every prerendered or rendered document: the title, the description meta tag, the attributes on <html> and <body>, the elements between two agent-ui-head comments at the end of <head>, and between two agent-ui-body comments at the end of <body>. A document written by the build is the template a per-request render fills in again, so writing twice gives the same document, and an attribute or element a later state no longer asks for is removed. The page's lang replaces the build's default lang="en"; an attribute the template has itself is replaced by the page's and is not restored when a later render stops asking, which is why every render starts from the shell (<name>.html), as the build and createSsrHandler do. A base is written at the end of <head>, so it does not change URLs written earlier in it (stylesheets in the template); put URLs that must follow it after, or write them absolute.

The browser keeps it current. The title always follows the state. The rest follows it through the plugin withHead (import { withHead } from '@ehtb/agent-ui/head', listed as plugins: [withHead]): the description, the attributes of <html> and <body>, and meta and link elements. A page that has such a value as a function of the state and no withHead is refused when it is defined, because the browser would keep the server's value without anyone saying so. A page with literals only, or whose changing parts are the title, downloads none of it. A script, style or base is written when the document is written (by the server, or by a soft navigation that copies it) and has literal attributes, so withHead never touches it; that includes the text of a data script built from the state (JSON-LD), which is the state at the moment the document was written and is not rewritten later. withHead re-reads the whole head on every change of any key, because a head function may read any of the state; it writes only what differs, so an unrelated write costs the head functions and not the document. A soft navigation (section 13, "Shell and soft navigation") copies the whole head of the document it fetched, including those elements, so a page reached by a soft link needs withHead only for what follows its state; a page that is not rendered on a server (the development server) has no such elements.

Text is escaped for where it goes. The text of a script of type application/ld+json, application/json, importmap or speculationrules may be built from the state (a string or any JSON value) and is escaped so no state value can end the script. The text of any other script, and of a style, is a literal string, and one that contains </script, </style or <!-- is refused.

Checked when the page is defined: unknown keys (with a suggestion), a tag that does not belong (title is head.title, a meta description is head.description, a charset is written by the framework), on* attributes (handlers are actions), a binding object where a function is meant, a function in a script, style or base, children on a meta or link, and a script with both src and children. At render an unsafe href/src stops with the attribute named.

Attribute names are lower case (charset, http-equiv, crossorigin, not charSet): HTML names are case-insensitive, and one spelling keeps the URL checks and the reserved-name checks exact. A name with an upper case letter is refused when the page is defined.
Not in head: the document's <meta charset>, the viewport, the page's stylesheets and the entry script. The build writes those.

title: Check
parts: agent-ui check (--config=<file>) renders every page in development mode, a page with parameters at the URLs its view.js lists in paths. It reports spec problems, action and resource errors, data that never loaded, missing titles, an invalid status, links that lead nowhere, and what the bundler refuses in the source (a re-export or export *, a default import or export in the project's own files, an import that does not resolve, an import cycle: BUILD.md, "Supported source dialect"; Node imports such a file, so only reading it as the bundler does finds it, with its file and line, once however many pages import it) in one list, and exits with code 1 when anything is wrong. The source is read once and every problem in it is reported, so a broken file costs a check no more than a good one. It renders a few URLs at a time (a small fixed bound) and keeps the report in page and URL order; a page that never becomes ready costs one renderTimeoutMs wait per batch rather than one per page, and a fetchFunction that keeps mutable state sees requests interleaved, as it would on a server. A link message lists at most ten pages. It prints a table of what each URL it rendered costs: the elements shown (page and shell), the rows of the largest list, the bytes of the state script. budgets in build.config.mjs (stateBytes, elements, listRows) turn a page over a limit into a problem (BUILD.md, "Budgets"). checkProject returns the same numbers as measurements.

title: 14. Limits and what is deliberately not here
parts: Not built, with reasons (details in DESIGN.md):
Component instances with their own state or lifecycle. Use expandComponents for markup and a namespace mounted under several names for state logic.

A modal, popover, menu or tooltip component with a focus trap. A native dialog plus explicit state is the one form; copy recipe modal, whose plugin traps and restores the focus and marks the background inert.
Refs in the view, and effects that are not a resources entry or a plugin. A plugin claims an element with mountElement.
Scoped CSS or CSS-in-JS. Plain stylesheets keep selectors greppable.
A template language. The spec is the template language.
Two-way binding sugar. An explicit one-line action keeps one writer path.
Directive systems.
Node-adopting hydration. Replacement keeps one render path.
Patching a module in place. agent-ui dev swaps a whole page instead (section 12), starting it from the state the old one had.
Non-DOM renderers.

A session store, an auth flow, a CSP policy or a cache layer. createSsrHandler exposes the request and three hooks (initialStateFor, stateForBrowser, transformResponse); the project owns the cookie format, the login route and the policy. Shipping one would choose them for every app.

Streaming server rendering and partial hydration. A page is rendered to one string after it is ready (or answered 503 on timeout by default); there is no stream of earlier markup and no hydration of a partial tree. The state script is the whole handover.

File uploads, streaming request bodies, Server-Sent Events and WebSocket endpoints. createSsrHandler reads a JSON or URL-encoded body once, up to maxBodyBytes; a host that needs multipart, a raw stream or a long-lived connection receives it in its own route and passes parsed data as request.body, or serves it beside the handler.

Internationalization and right-to-left layout as framework features. Text and direction are ordinary state and attributes; a project decides how it translates, stores a locale and sets dir. The framework ships no message catalogue and no locale-aware URL scheme.
A cross-page transition, and scroll positions inside scrolling containers across a soft navigation (the window's position is restored on back and forward).

A built-in load benchmark or cross-browser test matrix. Cost is counted, not timed: measureAction/assertCost in tests, the page table of agent-ui check and the build, and budgets. A few tests drive Chrome; Firefox and Safari are not run.
Known limits:
Derived lists are recomputed in full (O(n)) when their dependencies change.
There is no virtualization. Very long lists render every row.
{item} in a nested each reads only the innermost row. An outer row is read with as and {row}.
A select's value is not re-applied when its options change after mount.
SVG is a closed subset for icons and simple drawings (section 3, "SVG"); no text, gradients, filters, canvas or media tags. Events are limited to the list in section 3.
tree() and outline() read the DOM, so they reflect what is rendered.
Typed-but-unsubmitted input and the focus are carried over when server markup is replaced, by data-id; scroll positions inside scrolling containers and running animations are not.
Proposed (not built): undo and redo on the action log, frozen derived outputs, a text rendering of outline() for review, and list virtualization if real apps need it.

title: Build & deploy
text: A build turns the folders below pages/ into a site in dist/ that any static host can serve. You get separate, readable JavaScript and CSS files, the agent-ui runtime as its own cacheable chunk, and one HTML page per page. Which pages exist is not configured: a folder with a page.js is a page and its path is its URL (GUIDE.md, section 1). The command treats the current directory as the project root, reads build.config.mjs there and looks for the pages in pages/. --config=<file> names another file. Every example in this repository has its own build.config.mjs to copy from. Three things to know up front: Names are never mangled. Production strips comments and indentation only. A real minifier can be plugged in through the transform option (examples/events shows esbuild), or run over dist/assets/ afterwards. The pipeline has no dependencies. It needs Node 22 and nothing else, so it runs where npm installs are blocked. Pages are served over HTTP. A built site is served by a server, never opened from a file: agent-ui serve for development and tests, or your own server with createSsrHandler in production (see "Production checklist").

title: What gets built
parts: A page's file name is its URL with / replaced by - and the parameter marks removed: / is index, /event/:id is event-id. Two URLs that would give the same name are an error that names both. Pages contain no inline JavaScript or CSS. Asset URLs are root-absolute, so the site is served from the root of its domain. Hashed assets can be cached forever, and the dev server sends immutable headers for them. Changing a page changes only that page's chunk name. The runtime chunk, the framework's other chunks and every package's chunk keep their names and stay cached: an edit to the app's code never changes them. Tests cover this.

Next to the build output the project gets .agent-ui/, generated on every build and read again by check and serve: for each page a browser entry (main.js), a server module (app.js) and the page's finished spec (spec.js), generated from the folders, and for each shell (docs/API.md, section 13) its finished content once (shells/<name>.js, which the entries of its pages import, so it lands in a shared chunk). CSS entry points also get browser-only style modules (styles/<name>.js), one per file in the @import graph; they are the only modules that import CSS. A generated file is written only when its text changed, so a second load leaves an unchanged tree untouched; what a previous load wrote and this one did not (the folder of a deleted page, a shell no page uses, the files of a production build after a development one) is removed. app.js imports view.js and builds the spec in Node; main.js imports spec.js, the spec as data, so the browser never downloads the view. With --dev the browser entry imports view.js and builds the spec itself, because agent-ui dev never evaluates a page in Node and a page module imported there would go stale between rebuilds. .agent-ui/ ignores itself (it holds its own .gitignore); never edit it.

title: The finished spec
parts: A production build evaluates each page once in Node and ships its finished spec (view, pending view and layout) as data in spec.js. Before writing it, the build checks it with the validator, so the message names the page and a production browser bundle does not need the validator. The browser builds its DOM from that spec exactly as it did when it built the spec itself; what changed is only that the code that assembles the spec (the builders, components and layouts) stays in Node. A page whose view.js throws, or whose spec is not valid, fails the build with the page's name and the fix. A view.js that exports a name other than view, layout or pending fails the same way, with the nearest valid name. Node keeps modules for the life of a process: a second build in the same process (a test or a script, not the agent-ui command) evaluates an edited page.js or view.js again, but not the modules those import, so start a new process for a change deeper down.

title: The four stages
parts: Each stage is a plain function in build/, usable and testable on its own inside the repository; the package exports @ehtb/agent-ui/build and the stages build, config, presets and prerender. build/build.mjs wires them together. In front of the stages, build/pages.mjs (run by loadConfig) finds the pages in the folders, checks them, writes the generated entries to .agent-ui/ and hands the bundler a list of entries ({ name, path, url }); build() also accepts such a list written by hand, which is how the tests and scripts use the stages alone.
Stage   File   Job

1. Module graph   parse-module.mjs, module-graph.mjs   Parse every module reachable from the entries (the dialect is listed below), resolve imports, order modules dependencies first, detect cycles. Dynamic import() targets become extra roots.
2. Chunk plan   assign-chunks.mjs   Decide which modules are bundled together (rules below).

title: How chunks are chosen
parts: Manual chunks win. manualChunks in build.config.mjs maps a chunk name to path patterns. frameworkBuildOptions, from @ehtb/agent-ui/build/presets.mjs, puts the core runtime in a chunk named agent-ui, so every page loads it as a separate, cached file. Plugins such as resources.js and window-events.js are deliberately not listed. They are chunked by use, so a page only downloads the plugins it imports. Patterns support * within a directory and ** across directories.

Everything else is grouped by who needs it and whose code it is. Each module is tagged with the set of roots that reach it (roots are the pages and dynamic import() targets) and with its layer: the framework (agent-ui's own src/), one npm package, or the app (everything else, including .agent-ui/). Modules with the same set and the same layer share a chunk:
the app's code of one page: a chunk named after it, such as index or event-id; of one lazy root: a lazy chunk named after the file, such as devtools;
the app's code of several roots: a shared-<names> chunk, downloaded once and cached;
the framework's code outside the core: agent-ui-<names>, such as agent-ui-checkout-index-product-id (pages, hydration, resources, the shell);

a package: vendor-<package>, such as vendor-chart.js or vendor-kurkle-color for @kurkle/color. When pages use different parts of one package, each part is vendor-<package>-<names>. Two packages that import each other cannot be two files: their code of the same pages is one vendor-<names> chunk.

<names> is the list of roots, or its hash when the list is longer than 48 characters. The point of the layers is caching: the framework and the packages change when you upgrade them, the app's code on every deploy, and a file that holds both would be downloaded again for either.

Small chunks are folded together. Grouping by the exact set of pages and the layer makes up to one chunk per combination, which on a site of many pages would be dozens of tiny files. A chunk that is not a root's own and is below minSharedChunkBytes (default 4096 bytes of JavaScript and CSS source; 0 turns it off) joins a chunk whose pages include all of its own: one of the same layer when there is one, otherwise one of the app's, never a framework chunk or a package's chunk of the other layers. Among those it picks the one with the fewest pages, then the biggest. The chunk says so in its reason. The pages that did not need that code download it too: a few kilobytes in exchange for one request fewer. A fold that would make two chunks import each other is skipped.

A page loads its entry chunk and that chunk's static dependencies. Dependencies come first and are listed as modulepreload hints. Lazy chunks are fetched by import() when needed. The CSS of eager chunks is linked in the page: global CSS first, then imported/shared CSS, then the page's own page.css. The CSS of a lazy chunk is injected by the chunk when it loads.
The chunk graph must be acyclic. Automatic grouping guarantees it. A bad manual split is reported as chunk cycle: x -> main -> x with the advice to adjust manualChunks.

title: Pages and chunks
parts: Splitting is by page, and it is automatic: every page is an entry, so a page downloads the code it imports and the code its pages share, and nothing else. What to do with it:

Import what a page uses, from the module that defines it. Whole modules are included (no tree shaking), so write one component per module and import it by path. A file that re-exports many components (index.js) would put every component in every page, and re-exports are a build error in this dialect.
Put what several pages use in a module they all import (a layout, a shared namespace, shared components). It lands in a shared- chunk that is downloaded once and cached.
List a namespace only on the pages that need it. Its resources run on every page that lists it, and its code ships in that page's chunks.
List the plugins a page needs (plugins: [withResources]): a page without data does not download the resources code.

Page styles go in page.css next to the page; styles of every page go in pages/style.css. Both may @import other .css files: a file imported by two pages is one shared stylesheet linked only to those pages, and one imported by every page comes through pages/style.css. See "CSS imports" below.

Keep the builders out of page.js. @ehtb/agent-ui/spec and defineElement build the spec in Node, for view.js. When a module that page.js imports reaches them, a production build still works but prints warning: src/spec.js is in a browser bundle (the chain of imports); move what imports them into a module that only view.js imports. A --dev build is not checked (its entries import view.js on purpose).

The manifest lists the size of every module in each chunk (moduleSizes, bytes of source) and the CSS files that make up a chunk (stylesheetSources), so you can see what a file costs and what a page pulls in. Each page also lists its stylesheet URLs in order (stylesheets) and their total size (stylesheetsSize).

examples/shop is the model: three pages, a shared layout, cart and components, a cart on the server, and build.test.mjs asserting what each page loads. Its README has the measured sizes of every chunk (plain, gzip, esbuild, esbuild + gzip), what is downloaded once and what per page, how the split works step by step, and the limits.
No module is ever duplicated, so module state such as singletons behaves exactly as in the source.

What to do with it: Import what a page uses, from the module that defines it. Whole modules are included (no tree shaking), so write one component per module and import it by path. A file that re-exports many components (index.js) would put every component in every page, and re-exports are a build error in this dialect. Put what several pages use in a module they all import (a layout, a shared namespace, shared components). It lands in a shared- chunk that is downloaded once and cached. List a namespace only on the pages that need it. Its resources run on every page that lists it, and its code ships in that page's chunks. List the plugins a page needs (plugins: [withResources]): a page without data does not download the resources code. Page styles go in page.css next to the page; styles of every page go in pages/style.css. Both may @import other .css files: a file imported by two pages is one shared stylesheet linked only to those pages, and one imported by every page comes through pages/style.css. See "CSS imports" below. Keep t

title: CSS imports
parts: page.css and pages/style.css are CSS entry points. They may start with relative imports:

The build resolves every import at build time, removes the @import statements from the CSS it ships, and writes a browser-only style module for each file. The module imports its own imports first and the file's CSS last, so dependencies come before the rules that use them. The page entry imports the page.css module; global.js imports the pages/style.css module. No page.js, view.js or component module imports CSS.

A CSS file imported by pages A and B is reached by both entries, so the existing chunk plan puts it in one shared stylesheet for those two pages. A file imported from pages/style.css is loaded by every page. A file imported by one page stays in that page's chunk. minSharedChunkBytes counts CSS bytes, so a large shared stylesheet is not folded into an all-pages chunk merely because its generated module is small. A tiny shared file may still be folded into a bigger shared chunk, exactly as small JavaScript chunks are.
The accepted form is one statement per import, at the top of the file, before rules and other at-rules:
The path is relative and ends in .css; a URL, a package name, url(...), and layer, supports or a media query on the import are refused with a fix. Put a media query inside the imported file.
Imported files may import further files. Cycles are refused with the chain.
@import after another rule is refused; the build does not leave it for the browser to fetch.

Order is global CSS first, imported files before their importer, and page.css last, so a page rule can override a shared component rule. For unrelated shared files whose order matters, use @layer or keep them in one importer.
CSS stays global: importing a component's stylesheet includes it in the pages that import it; it does not scope its selectors. Use a naming convention such as ui-alert.

A page that uses only shared CSS can have a page.css with only @import statements. agent-ui check reports a missing file, a late import and a cycle when it loads the page folders; a production build does the same before it writes the site.

title: Supported source dialect
parts: The bundler has no JavaScript parser. It accepts the subset below, and each statement must start at the beginning of a line.
Allowed   Notes
import './file.js';   Side-effect import. The extension is required.

import './file.css';   Stylesheet, extracted per chunk and concatenated in module order. In page.css and pages/style.css, a top-level @import "./file.css"; is resolved by the build (see "CSS imports"); JavaScript never imports a page's CSS.
import { a, b as c } from './file.js';   May span lines.
import * as ns from './file.js';
import('./file.js')   String literal only. Creates a lazy chunk.

import { a } from 'package', 'package/subpath'   Resolved through node_modules, or the package importing itself, and the package's exports map with the import and default conditions and one * wildcard. The target must be an ES module .js, .mjs or .css file. This is how agent-ui itself is imported.
export const function class name, export { a, b as c };   Exports must not be reassigned elsewhere, because imports are bound once.

import name from 'x', import name, { a } from 'x', import name, * as ns from 'x', export default ...   In files of a package only, so code you cannot change can be bundled: the file a package import ('package', 'package/subpath') resolves to, including a linked, file: or workspace package whose real path is outside node_modules, and the files it imports by relative path (the project importing itself by its own package name is not a package). The default export is the key default of the module's exports (import { default as name } and export { name as default } are the same thing). A named function or class declaration keeps its name; any other export default value is assigned to a local called moduleDefault (moduleDefault2, ... if the file already uses that name). The project's own files keep one form: named exports only.

These are build errors that name the file and the line (lib.js:12: ...): default imports and exports in the project's own files (they are accepted in a package), export * from, re-exports (also in a package), the same export name twice, an import or export that does not start its line, export let and export var, destructuring exports, bare specifiers that name no installed package or no exported path, node: built-ins, imports of other file types, missing files, and import cycles. agent-ui check reads the modules the same way and reports them too, so they are found before a build or agent-ui dev refuses them.

Statements are found in code only: an import or export written in a comment, a string or a template literal is not a dependency and not an error. Regular expression literals are skipped where one can start after an operator, (, , or return; after ) or ] a / is read as a division.
Not detected: top-level await. Module bodies are wrapped in a synchronous function, so it would fail when the chunk loads.

title: Vendor files: a package the dialect cannot read
parts: Some packages (zod, Tiptap, ProseMirror) are written with export * and re-exports, which the bundler rejects. Your source still imports the package by name (import * as z from 'zod/mini'; Node and tsc read the real package). Only the browser bundle gets a one-file build of it, through replaceModules. The recipe, as examples/with-typescript does it for zod:

vendor/zod-entry.js is the only file the tool reads. It names exactly what the app uses: export { array, enum, nullable, number, object, string } from 'zod/mini';. Name the exports, never export *: the tool then leaves the rest of the package out (export * put all of zod, 420 kB, in the file; the names above give 32 kB).

A vendor script of the project writes vendor/zod.js with esbuild, a devDependency of the project: esbuild vendor/zod-entry.js --bundle --format=esm --outfile=vendor/zod.js. Do not pass --minify: the bundler finds an import or export only at the start of a line, so a one-line file fails with unsupported import/export syntax (the build option transform minifies the finished chunks). The output is generated: do not commit it (.gitignore), and let the project's build and test scripts run vendor first.

build.config.mjs maps the package's file to the generated one: replaceModules: { ...options.replaceModules, 'node_modules/zod/mini/index.js': 'vendor/zod.js' } (the key is the file the import resolves to; the chunk report lists it). Keep vendor/ beside pages/, not in it.
A new function from the package means a new name in the entry, and running the script again. TypeScript needs nothing: it reads the package's own types.
The generated file is third-party code: the framework imports nothing from it, and the project owns the version it bundles.

title: Configuration (build.config.mjs)
parts: Key   Meaning
manualChunks   { chunkName: [patterns] }.

minSharedChunkBytes   Chunks that are not a page's own and are smaller than this many bytes of JavaScript and CSS source are folded into a bigger chunk (default 4096; 0 keeps one chunk per combination of pages and layer). See "How chunks are chosen".
outDir, assetsDir   Output locations, default dist and assets. Files below assetsDir are served with immutable caching, and manifest.json records the name.
hash   Content hashes in file names, default true.

sourceMaps   true writes a <chunk>.js.map next to every chunk and ends the chunk with //# sourceMappingURL=...; the manifest lists it as sourceMap. Default false. See "Source maps". agent-ui build --source-maps turns it on for one build. With transform, the transform returns its own map (below).
minify   Strip comments and layout whitespace from JavaScript and CSS. Names are never changed, so the output stays greppable and stack traces readable. Off in --dev.

transform   (code, { file, kind, sourceMap }) => result, run after minify on every chunk. kind is 'javascript' or 'css', file the chunk's name. sourceMap is true for a JavaScript chunk when sourceMaps is on: the transform then returns { code, map }, its code and its own source map (an object or its JSON); otherwise it returns the code as a string. Any other result is a build error with the fix. Plug a real minifier in here, for example esbuild's transformSync(code, { minify: true, format: 'esm' }).code. examples/events/build.config.mjs does this for production builds only, with source maps (transform: dev ? undefined : ..., with loader: 'css' for stylesheets): the runtime chunk goes from 48.1 KB to 25.2 KB (gzip 13.0 to 10.3 KB). Names of exports and imports between chunks are kept, so chunks still load each other. The minifier is the project's own devDependency; the framework imports nothing.

replaceModules   { 'src/validate.js': 'build/stubs/validate-omitted.js' }: use another file's source for a module. This is how the validator, the runtime's own message checks (src/runtime-checks.js), the builders' checks, the page checks and the checks of shells and syncApps are left out of production builds, and the server-only half of pages (src/pages-server.js) out of every browser bundle.

api   Path of a Node module exporting createApi({ root }): the project's JSON endpoints and form handlers. Used by agent-ui serve for the HTTP endpoints. It does not answer the page's own data requests while rendering; fetchFunction does.

fetchFunction   (url, init) => Promise<response>: answers the data requests a page makes while it is rendered on the server (agent-ui build --static, agent-ui check, agent-ui serve). There is no default source of data; a page that fetches while rendering needs one (files, an in-process API, a running server). See "Data while rendering".

renderTimeoutMs   How long a page that declares ready may take to become ready while it is rendered. Default 2000. A static build fails on timeout; createSsrHandler answers 503 unless its own onTimeout says otherwise.

stateForBrowser   (state, request) => state: which state the document's state script carries after the page rendered. Keep the page's namespaces and keys; remove a server-only key. The markup is rendered from the full state, and a declared default is in the browser bundle. The request is null during a static build and agent-ui check.

basePath   The path the site is served below, for example '/shop' (default: the root). Specs, page folders, route.path, resources and the API keep the site's own paths; the build, the runtime, the render server and soft navigation add or remove the base on the wire. See "A site below a base path".
budgets   { pageGzipBytes?, stateBytes?, elements?, listRows? }: limits that turn a page over them into an error. pageGzipBytes fails the build; the others are agent-ui check problems. See "Budgets".

publicDir   Directory copied as it is to the output root (a symbolic link in it is refused: it would publish what it points to), so public/data.json becomes /data.json. Use it for data files and images that pages fetch by URL.

The configuration is checked before anything runs. An option that is not in this table fails with the list of allowed options and, for a near miss, Did you mean "outDir"?. A value of the wrong kind says what to write. The build deletes its output directory first, so it refuses an outDir that is the project root, that lies outside it, or that contains the pages, a publicDir or a package.json.

The pages are not in this table because nothing configures them: the folders below pages/ are the pages. Optional files next to the pages: pages/style.css (styles of every page); beside a page.js, its view.js (the content) and page.css (that page's styles). Both CSS files may @import shared CSS files (see "CSS imports").
Command line options are checked too. Every command lists the options it accepts:
Command   Options
agent-ui build   --config=<file>, --dev, --validator=include\ omit, --out=<directory>, --source-maps, --static (also write every page as a file; see "Static site")
agent-ui dev   --config=<file>, --port=<number>, --host=<address>
agent-ui serve   --config=<file>, --out=<directory>, --port=<number>, --host=<address>
agent-ui check   --config=<file>
agent-ui schema [outputFile]   none
agent-ui explain [name]   none; one optional name of a recipe or topic
agent-ui init   none

serve and dev listen on 127.0.0.1 (this machine) unless --host says otherwise: --host=0.0.0.0 is the explicit choice to serve the network. A server on this machine answers only to its own names (localhost, 127.0.0.1, [::1]) in the Host header and refuses any other with 421, so a web page cannot read the project through a rebound DNS name (hosts option of createStaticHandler and createSsrHandler; null, the default, answers to any). A 500 tells the visitor internal server error and nothing else; the error goes to the server's onError (default console.error), and every answer carries x-content-type-options: nosniff.
A misspelt or unknown option, a missing value, a port that is not a number, or a value outside the choices stops the command with exit code 2 and one line that names the option and the fix.

title: Production vs development builds
parts: build.config.mjs exports a function of the mode. build/presets.mjs exports frameworkBuildOptions({ dev, validator }), which returns the runtime chunk, the validator handling, and the minify and hash settings for both modes. Spread it into your config and add publicDir and the rest.
Mode   What you get

Production: agent-ui build   Comments and indentation stripped, about a quarter of the runtime's bytes. src/validate.js is replaced by a stub, so specs are not validated at mount; each page's finished spec is validated at build time instead (build/pages.mjs), and grammar is empty. The runtime chunk is about 40 KB raw and 11 KB gzipped (README.md has the sentence a test keeps true).
Development: agent-ui build --dev, agent-ui dev, all tests   Readable output with stable names. The validator is kept as a chunk of its own, named validator.
Validation exists to catch mistakes while writing specs, so ship without it. The exception is an app that generates specs at runtime in the browser: build it with agent-ui build --validator=include.

The stripper, build/strip.mjs, is a small scanner that understands strings, template literals, regex literals and comments. It keeps newlines, so automatic semicolon insertion is unchanged. Unit tests cover it.

title: Source maps
parts: sourceMaps: true (or agent-ui build --source-maps) writes <chunk>.js.map next to every chunk, so a stack trace or a breakpoint in a production bundle points at the source file and line. How they are made, because it decides what they can do:

The bundler keeps the lines of every module: an import or export statement that is taken out leaves its lines behind, empty, and the stripper keeps empty lines (it drops them only when sourceMaps is off). The map therefore says, for each output line, which line of which file it is. There are no columns: nothing is renamed or reflowed, and the line is what a debugger needs. The stripped output is a little larger with maps on (empty lines), by the number of comment-only lines.

sources names the files as the build read them (a module replaced by a stub is named by the stub), and sourcesContent embeds their text, so a map works without serving the sources. The consequence: a map contains your readable source. Serve it only where that is fine, or keep it out of the public output.
The //# sourceMappingURL= comment is added after the file name is fixed, so a map never changes a hash.

With a minifier. A minifier plugged in with transform rewrites the lines this build wrote, so the build's own map no longer fits. With sourceMaps on, the transform is called with sourceMap: true for every JavaScript chunk and returns { code, map }: the minifier's map goes from what it wrote to the chunk it was given, and the build follows every position of it through its own lines to the source file, then writes the result as the chunk's map. A position keeps its column in the minified file (where a line holds many statements) and its name; in the source it points at the start of the line, because the bundler takes export and indentation out of a line. The map must be version 3 with one source (its input), and the code must not carry its own //# sourceMappingURL= comment: the build adds the one for the file it writes, after the hash. With esbuild:
Stylesheets get no map: a chunk's CSS is the project's files concatenated in order, with a /* path */ comment before each.
A construct the bundler does not understand is reported with the file and the line (lib.js:12: default exports are not supported in the project's own files ...), whether or not maps are on.

title: Rendering on the server per request (agent-ui serve)
parts: agent-ui build && agent-ui serve serves dist/ at http://127.0.0.1:8080. serve renders from the project's sources, so it needs them (and build.config.mjs) next to the build, and it refuses a build that is older than the sources (manifest.json records a hash of what the build read): run agent-ui build again. It cannot serve someone else's dist/. A request whose path matches a page's URL is rendered for the requested URL with the page's own create(): a request for /blog/post/2 arrives with that post in the HTML and its state embedded, and the browser app takes over from there. The page's ready(state) says when it has its data and status(state) the HTTP status, for example 404 for an item that does not exist. The built page is the template. Markup sits between <!--ssr:start--> and <!--ssr:end-->, and the state script is replaced on every request, so the static prerender and the per-request render share one path. Data requests the page makes, such as /articles.json, are answered by fetchFunction.

A page that declares ready gets renderTimeoutMs (default 2000) to become ready. createSsrHandler answers 503 when the deadline passes, because a half-loaded page must not be mistaken for a finished one; it logs the timeout through log. title: The request, the hooks and response headers
parts: createSsrHandler is a request adapter for the host's server: it renders pages, and its optional api is a bridge for JSON endpoints and no-JavaScript form posts, because a form's outcome is a rendered page. It is not an application server: leave api out and the host's own routes answer the endpoints. It will not grow uploads, sessions, SSE or WebSockets; those are the host's (SECURITY.md).

Every page, API and form answer of createSsrHandler starts from one request context: { method, pathname, search, query, headers, cookies, signal }. The page's render, api.handle, api.handleForm, initialStateFor, stateForBrowser, transformResponse and the page's data requests (fetchFunction(url, init, request)) all read that request data; cookies are raw values, not percent-decoded. signal aborts when the client closes the connection, and the render passes it to the resources and their data requests, so a visitor who leaves does not keep a query running. A rendered form outcome gives the page render, initialStateFor, stateForBrowser, transformResponse, its resources and data requests the outcome page's path and query with the POST's method, headers and cookies (docs/API.md, section 12).
Three options are hooks, not features. The framework ships no session store, login flow or CSP policy; the project decides, and the hook supplies the request data or the value:

initialStateFor(request) returns public state in the shape of ui.state(), written into the document. Keep a session token in an HttpOnly cookie, never in that state: the state is in the HTML and reaches the browser. Check the cookie, the Origin header or a CSRF token in the API or form handler that changes state.

stateForBrowser(state, request) returns the state the document's state script carries after the page rendered. Use it to leave out a key that only the server's own code reads, or to replace an internal value. It can remove a namespace or key but cannot add one, because the browser app would not have it declared. It is not a secret store: the markup was rendered from the full state, and a value in the page's declared default is in the browser bundle. Put server-only state in initialStateFor (and declare the key with an empty or neutral default) and leave it out here. During a static build the request is null.

transformResponse(request, { status, headers, body }) runs for every answer this handler writes once a request context exists: pages, API answers, form outcomes, its 404 and 500, and the 400 for a body it cannot read. It returns { headers?, body? } or null. Return only the headers to add or replace: the headers passed in contain the framework's own headers (for example content-type on a page or API answer) and its security header, and those names are refused in a returned object, so read them and do not spread them. A returned header replaces the existing one; set-cookie values add up; the framework's security header is merged last.

The body is a string and the hook returns the whole replacement. Add a CSP nonce to every inline script tag there, as above; the state-script reader and soft navigation accept attributes in any order, so hydration and soft links still work. A page's module script is external and covered by 'self'. A page's CSS is an external stylesheet covered by style-src 'self'; a page that emits inline style needs a hash, a nonce or 'unsafe-inline', which the host decides. A soft navigation copies the next page's head and body scripts; an inline script that differs is created and runs, but the fetched document's nonce belongs to that response, not to the CSP of the document that stays. Keep page behavior in its module entry or a plugin when a soft link is used; do not rely on an inline script there. The state script is data, not code. The body may be HTML, JSON or plain text: check headers['content-type'] before rewriting it.

Because the transform runs last, it can set a page's cache policy or CSP. Set a site policy unconditionally in the transform to make it a floor. It runs after the API or form outcome headers and the framework's cache default.

The hook does not run for a request that goes to next(), nor for the 421 and 400 answered before a request context exists. If it throws, the visitor gets a 500 and the hook is not run again on that answer.

A page GET is no-cache unless the transform sets a cache header; an API answer is no-store unless the endpoint or the transform sets one; the framework sets no-store on a form response and on the 4xx and 5xx answers the handler writes itself (a page's own status is a page answer), and a transform can replace that too (do not make a form response cacheable). A page whose state depends on the visitor should have the host send vary: cookie or cache-control: private from transformResponse for every answer.

Headers are checked in one place: names are lower case, a name given twice is an error, set-cookie is the only list, a line break, a control character other than a tab, or a non-ASCII character is refused, and the framework's own headers (content-type, content-length, content-encoding, x-content-type-options, the hop-by-hop headers) cannot be set. A page cannot set response headers. A host server or plugin that writes its own response can use the same checks with checkResponseHeaders and mergeResponseHeaders from @ehtb/agent-ui/http-headers (API.md section 12).
The reference app is examples/hydration. View its page source to see the difference.

This is a demo server. It has no compression, no streaming, no file-upload or multipart parsing, no SSE or WebSocket endpoints, and no error pages beyond a 500 with the message; transformResponse can set a cache policy, but the demo server itself does not cache. A real deployment puts those concerns in the host server.
text: createSsrHandler is a request adapter for the host's server: it renders pages, and its optional api is a bridge for JSON endpoints and no-JavaScript form posts, because a form's outcome is a rendered page. It is not an application server: leave api out and the host's own routes answer the endpoints. It will not grow uploads, sessions, SSE or WebSockets; those are the host's (SECURITY.md). Every page, API and form answer of createSsrHandler starts from one request context: { method, pathname, search, query, headers, cookies, signal }. The page's render, api.handle, api.handleForm, initialStateFor, stateForBrowser, transformResponse and the page's data requests (fetchFunction(url, init, request)) all read that request data; cookies are raw values, not percent-decoded. signal aborts when the client closes the connection, and the render passes it to the resources and their data requests, so a visitor who leaves does not keep a query running. A rendered form outcome gives the page render, initialStateFor, stateForBrowser, transformResponse, its resources and data requests the outcome page's path and query with the POST's method, headers and cookies (docs/API.md, section 12). title: Static files, forms and APIs
parts: A static site is not served by the framework. createStaticHandler sends files and the shell of a page for agent-ui dev; it does not map /about to about/index.html. Put the output of agent-ui build --static on a file host (nginx, a CDN, express.static), which does that itself.
Static files. Anything in public/ is copied as it is, so public/terms.html is served at /terms.html. A link to such a file is not a page, and agent-ui check accepts it because the file exists.

APIs and form posts. The config key api names a Node module exporting createApi({ root }). The object it returns has the members below. This is the plug-in point for a server side: any object with these members works. examples/events/compose-api.js builds one from per-page endpoint tables; examples/shop/api.js is a plain object; examples/with-express and examples/with-fastify leave the API to their host server.
apiBase, optional: the path below which handle answers GET requests (default '/api'). Any POST goes to handle, then to handleForm.

handle({ method, pathname, search, query, headers, cookies, signal, body }) for JSON endpoints. It returns { status, body, headers? } or { status, body, headers?, raw: true } for bytes it produced itself, or null. An API answer is cache-control: no-store unless it sets one, and it may set a cookie. With composeApi, a path that exists for other methods answers 405 with an allow header.

handleForm({ method, pathname, search, query, headers, cookies, form }), optional. It turns a plain HTML form post into { status, url, initialState?, headers? } or { redirect, headers? }. The first renders the page at url (a local path starting with /, not //, with no backslash or encoded separator at the start) with that state, so forms work without JavaScript. The second answers 303 with location and cache-control: no-store (post/redirect/get), so a reload does not post again; the redirect follows the same path rule, and its headers cannot set location or cache-control. A form response is no-store unless transformResponse replaces the cache policy. A POST to a path that is a page but that neither handle nor handleForm answers is a 404.

The API and the form handler receive the same request context as the page, and their headers follow the rules above. While a form outcome page is rendered, initialStateFor, stateForBrowser, transformResponse, its resources and fetchFunction see the outcome page's pathname, search and query; the method, headers and cookies remain those of the POST. A session token belongs in an HttpOnly cookie that one of them sets; the page only reads public state from initialStateFor. See API.md section 12 for the context, the header checks and the session hooks.

Request bodies are JSON or urlencoded, with a 100 KB limit. A body with no content type or another type (including multipart/form-data), or a compressed one (content-encoding), is answered 415, a body over the limit 413, and a malformed body 400; an empty body is {}. A host framework that parsed the body may pass it as request.body. An endpoint may answer { status, body, headers?, raw: true } to send bytes it produced itself (CSV, XML, a file); a raw answer must set its own content-type unless the body is empty. transformResponse runs for raw answers too (so site-wide headers still apply); it may rewrite a string body, but a binary body is sent unchanged and returning a body for it is refused. This is a demo server, and in-memory state is fine for a demo; it is not a production back end. A static host has no API: the generated pages still work, but a form needs JavaScript and a server to receive it.

title: Data while rendering
parts: A page that loads data (a resources entry) asks its fetchFunction for it, in the browser and while it is rendered on the server. In the browser that is fetch. On the server, the framework does not decide where the data comes from: fetchFunction in build.config.mjs does, and it is used by prerender, agent-ui check and agent-ui serve. It receives the same (url, init) as fetch and returns anything with ok, status, json() and text(); a Response works.

When a page is rendered for a request, fetchFunction receives the request context as its third argument (fetchFunction(url, init, request)), so it can forward the visitor's cookie or authorization header to the data source. prerender and agent-ui check have no request: the third argument is undefined there. A page whose data depends on the visitor is therefore not a page for a static build.

With no fetchFunction, the first data request while rendering fails with render: the page requested "<url>" but no fetchFunction is configured. Add ..., unless the URL is absolute (https://...), which goes to the real fetch. A page without resources never asks.

A host whose data is in its own process hands the handler a config with that function: createSsrHandler({ config: { ...config, fetchFunction } }) (examples/with-express, examples/with-fastify). The config is the only place a fetchFunction is given.

Files and in-process APIs are the project's own code. examples/directory/server-fetch.mjs reads public/ (the bytes the static host serves); examples/events/server-fetch.mjs also answers /api/ from the project's api module, in process.

title: Static site, hosting and the dev server
parts: A static site is agent-ui build --static: after the build every page is rendered with server/render-page.js from the page's generated module (the same create(env) the browser entry uses) and written to <path>/index.html (the page / to index.html), with its markup inside <div id="app">, followed by the state script, before the module script. A plain file host then serves finished pages with no server. It is for a site that names every page.

A page whose path has parameters (/event/:id, /docs/*path) is written once for every URL its view.js lists in paths: export const paths = ['/event/1', '/event/2'], or an async function that returns them (view.js runs only in Node, so it may read files or a database). Each URL must be a URL of the page, plain (letters, digits and . _ ~ - in its segments), and listed once. A page with parameters that lists none stops the build before it renders anything, naming the pages and the fix. agent-ui check renders the same URLs, so what is checked is what is written.
Data requests are answered by the fetchFunction of the config (see "Data while rendering"). Without one, the first request fails with the fix.
The page's ready says when its data is there. A page that never becomes ready fails the build instead of shipping a loading state.
A page whose data comes from a server that is not running during the build is not a page for a static site: build without --static.

Hosting. Asset URLs are root-absolute, below basePath when the config has one. There is always a server: agent-ui serve, or your own with createSsrHandler (API.md section 12), renders every URL that matches a page (for GET and HEAD), including the ones that were never generated.
Serving and checking.

agent-ui serve renders the pages per request (see "Rendering on the server"); a path that matches no page and no file is a 404. There is no catch-all page: a URL that should work is a page folder. (A page with a dot in the last segment, such as /user/jane.doe, is a page; only a known file extension makes a path a file.)
agent-ui dev swaps the edited page in place (hot reload, keeping its state) and rebuilds on change (API.md section 12). Pages render in the browser from their shells.

agent-ui check --config=<file> renders every page in development mode (a page with parameters at the URLs its view.js lists in paths) and lists problems without building (API.md section 13). It reads the modules the entries reach the way the bundler does, once, and reports every source problem a build would refuse (agent-ui build stops at the first). It renders a few URLs at a time (a small fixed bound), so pages that wait on data do not wait for each other; the report stays in page and URL order, and a page that never becomes ready costs one wait of renderTimeoutMs per batch instead of one per page. A fetchFunction that keeps mutable state therefore sees requests interleaved, as it would on a server that answers visitors at the same time. It prints what every page it rendered costs: the elements it shows, the rows of its largest list and the bytes of its state script; budgets turn a page over a limit into a problem. Requests to /api/ are answered by the project's api module, so a resource whose URL no endpoint answers is reported with the page that made it (each render keeps its own misses). It checks every link in a page's spec: a literal href that starts with / must be a page, a file in publicDir or an API path; a message lists ten pages at most, so one broken link on a site with a thousand pages stays readable.

agent-ui init writes the rules for agents into AGENTS.md of the project root, between <!-- agent-ui:start --> and <!-- agent-ui:end -->: the file is created when it does not exist, and when it does the block is added (or its own block replaced) and the rest is kept. The text is the block of the package's docs/AGENT-RULES.md (the root AGENTS.md is for work on the framework and is not published), so an agent that only reads the project's own file still learns the rules (the file in node_modules is not loaded by one). Run it again after an upgrade to refresh the block. agent-ui check prints a note when AGENTS.md does not mention agent-ui.
agent-ui schema [file] writes the JSON Schema of the spec grammar. The default is ./spec.schema.json in the current directory. In this repository npm run schema regenerates docs/spec.schema.json.

title: A site below a base path
parts: basePath: '/shop' serves the site at https://example.com/shop/. Inside the app nothing changes: a page folder is still pages/product/[id]/, a spec still writes a({ href: '/product/3' }), route.path is /product/3, a resource asks for /api/cart, and the project's API and fetchFunction see /api/cart. The base exists only on the wire:
the build writes the asset URLs below it (/shop/assets/...) and writes it into every browser entry;

the runtime writes it before every root-absolute URL it puts in the page (href, src, action, formaction, cite, each URL of ping and of srcset, and the same attributes in the head; a srcset URL that holds a comma is not supported), and the browser's fetch adds it to a resource's URL; a URL that is not root-absolute (https://..., //cdn..., #top, about) is left alone;

createSsrHandler answers only below the base (a request outside goes to next()), takes it off the path before it looks for the page, and adds it to a form's redirect; agent-ui serve and agent-ui dev serve the files below it;
soft navigation fetches the site's path, pushes the address with the base, and leaves a link outside the base to the browser.
CSS is not rewritten: a url() in a stylesheet is relative to the stylesheet (url(../images/a.png)), or carries the base itself.

title: Budgets
parts: budgets in build.config.mjs say how much a page may cost. Each is optional:
Limit   Measured by   What it counts

pageGzipBytes   agent-ui build   The JavaScript and CSS a first visit downloads before the page runs, each file gzipped (startupSize of the page in manifest.json, and the page table of the build report). Over it, the build fails after writing the site, naming the pages and their startup chunks.
stateBytes   agent-ui check   The bytes of the state script a rendered page carries.
elements   agent-ui check   The elements a rendered page shows, its shell's included.
listRows   agent-ui check   The rows of the largest list of a rendered page. Every row is rendered: there is no virtualization, so a long list is a page of the data at a time.

Without budgets the numbers are still printed: the build report has a table of pages with their startup size, and agent-ui check a table of every URL it rendered. What one action costs is measured in tests with measureAction and assertCost (API.md, "Testing").

title: Production checklist
parts: A build is not a deployment. Before a real site goes out:

Minify. agent-ui build strips comments and indentation and keeps names readable, so a stack trace in a production bundle still points at a function you can find. Plug a real minifier into transform for production only: examples/events/build.config.mjs does, and its runtime chunk goes from 48.1 KB raw / 13.0 KB gzip to 25.2 KB / 10.3 KB. Names of imports and exports between chunks are kept, so the site still loads. For stack traces that point at your files, turn sourceMaps on and have the transform return the minifier's map (see "Source maps"); the maps hold your source, so serve them only where that is fine, or upload them to your error tracker and keep them out of the public output.

Compress. Neither agent-ui serve nor createStaticHandler sets content-encoding: they are development and test servers. Put nginx (gzip or brotli), a CDN or the host's compression middleware in front, and check the transfer size of the largest chunk, not its size on disk.

Cache. Files below assetsDir have content hashes in their names and the framework's handlers serve them as immutable. HTML is no-cache unless transformResponse says otherwise; an API answer is no-store unless the endpoint or transformResponse says otherwise; the framework sets no-store on a form response and on the 4xx and 5xx answers the handler writes itself (a page's own status is a page answer), and a transform can override it (do not make a form response cacheable). A page whose state depends on the visitor should have the host send vary: cookie or cache-control: private from transformResponse: no-cache alone does not separate visitors in a shared cache. manifest.json names every chunk and the page that loads it.

Serve with the host. A deployed site is served by the host's own server (createSsrHandler in Express, Fastify or Node, or a static host for a --static build), not by agent-ui serve: the host owns TLS, compression, caching, logging and error pages. examples/production-server/server.mjs is a dependency-free model: the built files from memory, createSsrHandler for every page, security and cache headers, /healthz and graceful shutdown.

Set headers and a session at the host. createSsrHandler gives the request to initialStateFor, stateForBrowser and transformResponse; use them for a CSP, HSTS, a site-wide cookie and the public part of a session. Keep the session token in an HttpOnly cookie set by the API or a form, not in the state the document carries, and check it in the handler that changes state. A key only the server reads belongs in state added by initialStateFor with a neutral declared default, and is removed by stateForBrowser; that keeps it out of the state script but not out of markup the page renders. The framework writes no CSP, session store or CSRF policy. Set maxBodyBytes to the largest form or JSON body the host accepts (default 100 KB), and timeoutMs (or renderTimeoutMs in the config) to a budget the page's data can meet; the default 503 on timeout is deliberate.

Accept only the bodies you parse. The handler reads JSON and URL-encoded bodies, uncompressed; it answers 415 for another content type, including multipart/form-data, and for a compressed body (decode it in the host's body parser), 413 for a body over maxBodyBytes, and 400 for a body it cannot parse. A file upload belongs in a route of the host server, which passes the parsed value as request.body; the framework has no upload parser. The handler has no streaming, SSE or WebSocket endpoint: serve those from the host as well.
Do not edit dist/. Change the source and rebuild.

title: Adding things
parts: A new page: create pages/<url>/page.js exporting page and pages/<url>/view.js exporting view (GUIDE.md, section 3). It is picked up automatically; nothing else changes.
A lazy feature: import it dynamically, import('./devtools.js').then(...), from any module. It becomes its own chunk, and its CSS loads with it. Do not list it in manualChunks, or it becomes eager.
Shared app code: import the same file from several pages. It lands in a shared-... chunk automatically (small ones are folded together, see "How chunks are chosen").

title: Limits
parts: The pipeline leaves these out on purpose, to stay dependency free:
no tree shaking: whole modules are included;
source maps are opt-in (sourceMaps: true), one per JavaScript chunk, precise to the source line (not the column); with transform, the minifier supplies its map;
no identifier mangling: comments and whitespace only, use transform for a real minifier;
no CSS processing beyond resolving page.css/pages/style.css @imports and concatenating the files of a chunk: no URL rewriting, no scoping, no nesting, no autoprefixing;
no in-place patching of a module: the dev server swaps the whole edited page, with its state (API.md section 12);
no JSON imports, CommonJS packages or imports maps.
If you need them, use a full bundler and keep the same source layout.

title: Components
text: For an agent that has been given a React component (usually from shadcn/ui) and must produce the agent-ui version. Read AGENT-RULES.md (in this folder) first, then API.md section 12 (components, features, hooks table). The working reference is examples/react-converted-components: seven converted shadcn/ui components, their quoted originals, and the tests that compare the two. The result of a conversion is a component definition ({ params, spec }) in ui/<name>.js, state logic as a feature when the original has state, and tests that prove it matches the original. A conversion is finished when node --test passes in the example folder, not when it looks right.

title: 1. Quote the original
parts: Copy the React source into the top comment of ui/<name>.js, unchanged, between the markers the parity tests read:

Rules: one // Source: .../<file>.tsx line per quoted file, the code lines start with //, blank lines are //, and // (end of the quoted source) closes the block. Keep the licence line. If the original changes upstream, replace the quote; the parity tests then show what no longer matches.

title: 2. Take inventory
parts: Read the original and list every item below that it uses. Each one has a fixed answer in section 3.
Elements and tags. Which element carries each data-slot (or the root)?
Variants. cva groups (variant, size), their keys, their defaultVariants.
className and cn(...). Extra classes from the caller.
Props. Every prop the component reads, and what ...props forwards to the element.
children. What goes inside.
Events. onClick, onChange, and so on.
State and effects. useState, useReducer, useMemo, useEffect, useRef, useContext, custom hooks.
Polymorphism. asChild, Slot, a tag or as prop.
Primitives. Anything imported from @radix-ui, radix-ui, @base-ui or similar.
Icons, portals, animation, refs.

title: 3. Decide each item
parts: In the original   In agent-ui   Notes
root element, data-slot="x"   tag and props: { 'data-slot': 'x' }   Keep the same tag as upstream. The parity test fails if you change it.

cva({ variants: { variant: { default: "..." } }, defaultVariants })   params.variant: { options: { default: 'ui-x--default' }, default: 'default' }   Same keys, same order, same default. The value is your class name; the Tailwind strings are not copied.
data-variant={variant}, data-size={size}   'data-variant': { param: 'variant', key: true }   key: true gives the key the use wrote, not the mapped class.
cn(base, variants, className)   class: { join: ['ui-x ', { param: 'variant' }, ' ', { param: 'class' }] } and class: { default: '' }   A join of literals is folded at build time and tidied.
children   children: { slot: 'children' }   Use children: on the use node. There is one slot.
a node passed as a prop (icon, action)   params.action: { optional: true } and { param: 'action' } where it goes   The value is a whole node, for example { use: 'button', ... }.
onClick, onChange   params.onClick: { optional: true }, on: { click: { param: 'onClick' } }   The value is ['actionName', { args }].
...props   nothing   Declare every prop the component should accept. An undeclared prop is an error, which is the point. List the ones you drop in the header comment.
disabled, placeholder, type   a param: disabled: { default: false }, placeholder: { optional: true }   Optional with options and no default means the attribute is absent unless given.
id, htmlFor, aria-*   id: { optional: true }, for, 'aria-label' params   The validator requires aria-label on every input, so make it a required param.
useState   a feature: state key plus an action   See section 5.
useMemo, derived values   derive in the feature
useEffect fetching   a resources entry in the feature
useRef, forwardRef   none   Give the element an id.
useContext, providers   the global store
asChild, Slot   not supported   Write a second component for the other tag. Record it in the header comment.
@radix-ui Label   label with for   Native.
@radix-ui Checkbox   input with type: 'checkbox' and data-state   Native. Record the divergence (section 6).

Dialog, Popover, Select, Tooltip, Dropdown, Tabs, Accordion   native dialog, details/summary, select, or a feature with explicit open state   The behaviour behind them (open state, the active option, the displayed month, the row being moved) becomes a namespace, and the component binds to it. What is still not reproduced: a portal (content renders in place and CSS positions it), true focus trapping (a focus index plus the focus prop stands in), and library positioning. Say so in the header and in DESIGN.md. Do not fake it. The popover, combobox, date picker and drag list in examples/react-converted-components are worked examples.
icons (lucide-react)   text, or a children node   There is no icon library.
animation classes   transition plus CSS
When an item has no row, stop and say so rather than invent a mapping.

title: 4. Write the definition
parts: The export keeps the upstream name (Badge); the string is the name a raw { use: 'badge' } node writes. A page calls Badge({ variant: 'secondary' }, 'New'), and a misspelt param fails at that call. The raw { params, spec } object form still works for definitions written as JSON.
For a component that only wraps one element and a class, use container(name, baseClass, slot) from ui/define.js, which returns a defineElement component.
Add the component to ui/index.js as the made function, and name it with the upstream name with a lower-case first letter (CardTitle is defineElement('cardTitle', ...)).
Write the CSS for the classes you invented in style.css. Plain CSS with variables is enough; keep the class names greppable.

Variants are resolved when the page is built, so a variant is always a literal in a use node. To switch at runtime, write a when with one use per variant. A component that forwards its variant to another component declares its own options.

title: 5. State: the field namespace convention
parts: If the original keeps state or takes value and onChange, put that logic in features.js as a function that returns a namespace ({ state, derive, actions } with short names), mount it under the field's name (namespaces: { email: textField({ validate }) }), and have the component take a field name:
Piece   Name for field email
value   state email.value
left once   state email.touched, action email.touch
write   action email.set
message   derived email.error, email.invalid, email.message
checkbox   also derived email.state: 'checked' or 'unchecked'

The namespace name is the only prefix, so two fields never collide. The component builds the names with state(join(param('field'), '.value')). Two namespaces cannot share a name; mounting the same namespace under two names gives two independent copies.

title: 6. Prove it matches
parts: Parity against the quote. parity.test.mjs reads the quoted source. It already checks, for every quoted file: each exported component exists, variant and size keys and defaults are the upstream ones in the same order, and each data-slot is on the same element. Divergences are written down. If the conversion must use a different element or leaves something out, add it to DIVERGENCES with the reason. The test then also checks that upstream still renders what you said it does.

title: Design notes
text: Reader: an agent or human deciding whether and how to extend this. Working rules for an app author are in AGENT-RULES.md (in this folder), exact semantics in API.md, bundling in BUILD.md. Claims marked [hypothesis] are untested. Everything under "Evidence" was run in this repository.

title: 1. Thesis
parts: A UI framework does three things. It keeps the page in sync with the state. It offers aids for the person writing the code, such as components, template syntax, tooling and conventions. And it comes with an ecosystem. An agent needs the first, partly needs the third, and mostly does not need the second. agent-ui keeps the first small and explicit, and replaces the second with aids a machine can use: a closed grammar, a static validator, JSON introspection, typed actions, and deterministic replay.

The binding constraint in long agentic sessions is context decay. The agent forgets earlier decisions and edits code it has only partly read. So the design minimizes what must be remembered to make a correct edit.

Source is written in plain English names and is never minified by us. Minification is a separate, later process over the build output. It does not belong in the source or in the toolchain that agents read.

title: 2. Principles
parts: UI is data, not code. A JSON spec can be validated, diffed, patched and generated. There is no template syntax and there are no closures in the view layer.
Closed grammar, one way to say each thing. The node kinds are text, binding, element, each and when. Anything else is a validator error, not a new idiom.
Fail statically, locally, specifically. Defects the validator can see are reported as specPath: problem before mount. Runtime failures become data in errors.

Single source of truth, plain data. State is JSON in signals, updated immutably and frozen in development. Derived values are pure functions. There is no hidden state in closures, the DOM or instances.
One writer path. Only typed, named actions write state, and handlers hold no logic. That choke point gives logging, replay, validation, testing and exposure to external agents for free.
Determinism. The same initial state plus the same action log gives the same state and DOM. Ids and counters live in state. There are no clocks and no randomness in actions.
Fine-grained updates, no diffing. One effect per binding writes one DOM property. Keyed rows are reused. Events are delegated.
Observable by construction. State, derived values, action schemas, the log, errors and the interactive surface (tree()) are all JSON.
Stable addressing. data-id (explicit or spec path) and data-key (row key) identify elements in tests, logs and patches.
Native platform first, small enough to read. An agent that has read the runtime reasons from source, not from remembered semantics.
Constraint over flexibility. Add a feature only if it removes a class of errors or is unavoidable. Each addition in section 4 has a concrete need behind it.
Ship runtime and app separately. Pages load the runtime as a separately cached chunk plus their own small chunks and CSS files (section 3 and BUILD.md).

Accuracy over interpretation. The code states what to write and rejects everything else. Each shape is fixed: pages, API tables, build options. Unknown keys are errors with a suggestion, and every error says where, what, and the fix. An agent that follows the messages converges on the one valid form. agent-ui check runs all of it without a browser.
